Rail extension queried

By Mr. Pouliot:

subtopic: COMPENSATION TO PROVINCES IN LIEU OF CERTAIN TAXES

speakeroldname: Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: COMPENSATION TO PROVINCES IN LIEU OF CERTAIN TAXES
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 347, to authorize the government of Canada to enter into agreements with the governments of the
3548	HOUSE OF
Tax Agreements with Provinces provinces pursuant to which, in return for compensation, the provinces agree to refrain from levying certain taxes for a limited period.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as I explained at the resolution stage, the purpose of this bill is to authorize our entering into agreements with the provincial governments to make certain payments to them in return for the rental from them of certain tax fields for a further five-year period. I have also made it clear that the new agreements will be in substantially the same form as those which have been in effect with eight provincial governments during the past five fiscal years.
I believe the house would think it appropriate if I should now make a statement recalling some of the background and explaining the essential features of the new agreements.
It will be recalled that following protracted negotiations in 1945 and 1946, tax rental agreements were entered into with seven of the then existing provinces, that is, with all provinces except Ontario and Quebec, and later when Newfoundland entered confederation in 1949, a similar agreement was entered into with that province. Under these agreements, the details of which were the outcome of lengthy discussions, the provinces undertook not to levy during the five calendar years 1947 to 1951, or allow their municipalities to levy, personal income taxes, corporation income taxes, other taxes on corporations, or succession duties. In return for this undertaking, the federal government agreed to make rental payments during the five corresponding fiscal years-that is to say, the five fiscal years ending March 31, 1952- determined on the basis of certain formulae arrived at in joint discussions with the provincial governments. These rental payments were to be such as to guarantee to the province a fixed minimum level of payments, but this guaranteed minimum was to be adjusted upward to take account of national economic growth and increased provincial population. In practice, the actual payments made to the various provinces during the five years of the agreement exceeded by very substantial amounts the guaranteed minima.
Another feature of the old agreement involved the levy by each agreeing province of a tax of 5 per cent on corporation income earned within its jurisdiction. The purpose of this provision was to allow any non-agreeing province to tax its corporations up to this level without subjecting them to a tax burden higher than that being paid by corporations in the agreeing provinces.


In keeping with the same purpose, the federal government has so shaped its own succession duty program as to allow a credit up to one-half of the federal duties for duties paid to a non-agreeing province, and there has also been a standing offer to non-agreeing provinces to allow a credit against federal personal income tax up to 5 per cent for a personal income tax imposed by any nonagreeing province. Neither of the non-agreeing provinces has chosen to take advantage of this latter credit.
Before proceeding to discuss the provisions of the new agreement, I would like to express my own general satisfaction with the conditions that have prevailed in federal-provincial tax relations during the post-war period. Those provinces which entered into agreements have, I believe, been well compensated for renting certain of their tax fields to us and have been assured against the possibility of drastic declines in the yield of these important fields of direct taxation. This has enabled them to plan their own programs with greater assurance and has undoubtedly improved their credit in the financial markets. At the same time, a level of efficiency in over-all tax administration has been achieved hitherto unknown in this country. Furthermore, the non-agreeing provinces have shown a restraint in employing their taxing powers which has contributed in no small measure to achieving a national system of taxation which is almost free of overlapping administration and conflicting jurisdiction.
As already indicated, the old agreements with eight of the ten provinces expired on March 31 last. In anticipation of this event, the federal government called a conference in Ottawa in December, 1950, of all provincial governments to consider the terms of new agreements for the ensuing five-year period.
In return for the same provincial undertakings as in the old agreements, the federal government offered to provide guaranteed minimum payments at a level considerably higher than under the old agreements. I shall come to the details of this offer in a moment or two. These proposals were considered at the conference in discussions which were marked by the utmost cordiality but no final decisions were taken and the provincial representatives undertook to give the proposals further consideration.
During the course of 1951, I received certain counter-proposals from the provinces, all of which were given the most serious consideration and many of which we were able to accept. By means of discussion with representatives from individual provinces following which any changes were made known to all

the provinces, we have now succeeded in arriving at a basis of agreement which represents only a modification in detail of the proposals made to the 1950 conference. It is to implement this basis of agreement for which authority is requested in this bill. Up to the present time the indication is that at least the same eight provinces with which we have had agreements for the past five years will be entering into new agreements for the next five years.
With this general background, I shall now turn to a more detailed discussion of the main provisions of the proposed new agreements.
I shall deal first with the provincial undertakings, The provincial governments and their municipalities will, as in the old agreements, refrain from imposing personal income tax, the corporation income tax, the so-called corporation taxes-i.e. taxes on places of business, paid-up capital, etc.-and succession duties.
As in the case under the old agreements, any province has the option of retaining its succession duties if it so chooses, in which case, of course, there is provision for an offsetting reduction in its compensation. Actually, none of the provinces with which we have concluded agreements has accepted this alternative.
A change of some substance which was announced some time ago is that the agreeing province will no longer be required to levy a 5 per cent corporation tax. As explained in my budget speech, we are accomplishing the same general purpose by adding the 5 per cent tax-or practically all of it-to the federal rate and allowing a credit up to 5 per cent on corporation income earned within a nonagreeing province.
Under the old agreement, the agreeing provinces retained the full right to levy charges on their natural resources and to impose income taxes on mining income or on logging income. The federal government also undertook to allow a deduction for such provincial taxes from income subject to its corporation tax. These arrangements will be continued under the new agreement.
Provisions relating to the obligation of the federal government to pay compensation to the provinces are much more complicated and I must ask the house to bear with me in this rather involved exposition.
The guaranteed minimum payments under the new agreements are, with the exception of one additional formula, basically those of the expiring agreements adjusted upwards to a higher level. The old guaranteed minimum payments were established, by election of each province, on the basis of two general
Tax Agreements with Provinces alternative formulae. The relative advantages of these I discussed in detail when I introduced the 1947 legislation and I will not review them at this time.
Briefly, it might be said that one of these, through emphasis on a per capita payment, gave more prominence to the factor of fiscal need. This formula was as follows:
1.	$15 per capita on the 1942 population of the province, and
2.	the amount of the statutory subsidies payable to the province in 1947.
This option was most favourable for Nova Scotia, Saskatchewan and Newfoundland.
The second formula was designed to give more emphasis to the tax potential of a province. In it there were three elements, namely:
1.	50 per cent of the province's revenue from personal income taxes, corporation income taxes and corporation taxes, in the year 1940 as established for the purposes of the wartime tax agreements;
2.	$12.75 per capita on the 1942 population of the province; and
3.	The amount of the statutory subsidies payable in 1947.
This formula was more advantageous for all other provinces with the exception of Prince Edward Island for which a special guaranteed minimum payment of $2,100,000 was fixed.
In the proposals made at the 1950 conference, the federal government offered new guaranteed minimum payments on the basis of these formulae adjusted upwards by the ratio of change in provincial population and per capita gross national product between the year 1942 and the year 1948. In general, this "upping" of the payments to the 1948 basis had the effect of increasing the minimum payments by about 50 per cent. However, at the same time to meet the position of certain provinces which had argued that greater emphasis should be given to the element of tax potential, a new alternative formula was suggested.
The components of this new option were as follows:
1.	The estimated yield of a personal income tax at 5 per cent of 1948 federal rates applied to 1948 incomes in the province;
2.	The yield of a tax of 8J per cent on corporation profits earned in the province in 1948. This rebate of 8J per cent, I might explain, is taken as a fair measure of the corporation tax potential and takes account of the gross or specific taxes traditionally levied by provinces on corporations as well as taxes on corporate profits;

Tax Agreements with Provinces
3.	The revenue received by the province from succession duties in a recent 3-year period; and,
4.	Statutory subsidies payable to the province in 1948. In actual application, this formula proved to be of benefit only to the province of Ontario.
As a result of provincial representations subsequent to the conference, minor modifications in the calculation of the adjustment between 1942 and 1948 have been accepted, but essentially the new guaranteed minima are those offered by the federal government in December, 1950. To conclude this aspect of the matter, therefore, I will, with the permission of the house, place on Hansard a table showing the guaranteed minimum payments under the old agreements and the guaranteed minimum payments that will form the basis of agreements that will be authorized under the bill now before us.

Let me emphasize that the amounts I have included in the table are only the guaranteed minimum payments below which no actual payment may fall regardless of prevailing economic conditions or changes in population. The actual amounts payable in a given year -which, incidentally, we call the adjusted annual payments-are the result of calculations by which these guaranteed minimum payments are increased to give effect to national growth, as measured by the gross national product per capita, and to provincial growth, as measured by the provincial population.
Under the old agreements, the adjustment for these factors has been calculated as the average of ratios for the three years preceding

the year of payment in relation to the base year 1942. This three-year averaging had the effect of bringing greater stability into the adjusted payments by spreading out the effect of a sudden change in economic conditions. It has been represented to us, however, that in a period of very rapid growth such as we have been experiencing, the three-year averaging process may slow down unduly the increase in provincial revenue at a time when fairly rapid increase in those revenues may be needed because of rapid growth of provincial population. In order to meet this argument, we proposed in the December 1950 conference to provide in the new agreements for an averaging calculation based upon a two-year period rather than upon a three-year period. Subsequent representations have indicated that even this adjustment was not believed by some governments to be flexible enough, and early this year, in a letter to all the provincial governments, I proposed that a province should have the option of choosing either an adjustment based on a two-year average or one based simply on the data relating to the one year prior to the year of payment. In a period of expansion, the one year calculation obviously will result in a considerably higher immediate payment to provinces and perhaps it is not surprising, therefore, that all provinces so far have elected to accept this option.
Under the new agreements, therefore, the adjusted payments which we will make to any agreeing province, in each of the five fiscal years beginning with this fiscal year, will be based on the ratio of per capita gross national product and of provincial population in the year preceding the year of payment compared with the new base year, namely, 1948. To illustrate the effect of this new adjustment process, I would like, with the consent of the house, to place on Hansard a table comparing the guaranteed minimum payments that will be authorized for each province under the bill with the amount of the adjusted payment, as presently estimated, that will be payable in the first fiscal year of the new agreement, namely, 1952-53.
Perhaps I should add that the adjusted payments shown in this table include the statutory subsidies payable to the various provinces.

Another point of some significance to which I should call attention is that under the new agreements the adjusted payments to be made in respect of any one year will be paid in quarterly instalments within the fiscal year -June 30, September 30, December 31 and March 31. Under the old agreements the quarterly payments began on September 30 of the calendar year and the last one was made on June 30 of the following year. The house will note that, as a result of this change, the agreeing provinces will receive during the fiscal year 1952-53 the final or June 30 quarterly instalment in respect of the last year of the old agreement, and, in addition, the four quarterly instalments of the first fiscal year of the new agreements. This change was made possible by greater promptness in securing our estimates of gross national product and provincial population and is one which naturally is valued highly by the agreeing provinces.
Another change of minor significance is that in the new agreements the gross national product concept which we will use in calculating the adjusted payments will be that of gross national product at factor cost rather than gross national product based on market prices. This new concept has the advantage of eliminating indirect taxes levied in Canada, an element which reflects primarily the relative intensity of use of certain tax sources at any one point of time rather than the level of economic activity.
A feature of the 1947 legislation that will be continued in the future is the payment to the provinces of one-half of our corporate income tax collections, less certain deductions, from companies engaged in the generation or distribution of electric energy, gas or steam, in respect of their income derived from such generation or distribution. Under the authority of the existing act, payments have been made to all provinces whether or not they had entered into a tax rental agreement. In respect of incomes of the three

In view of the more precise determination of income derived from this class of public utility companies from the specified type of activities provided for under this year's amendments to the Income Tax Act, the payments to be made to provincial governments in respect of the next five years will, of course, vary somewhat from what those payments would have been had the old methods of calculation been followed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the motion was before this house that it was expedient to introduce this measure I placed on record my opinion in regard to the unsatisfactory situation which is created by the extension of these agreements with no assurance that we will at some point tackle the fundamental problem which makes it necessary to have agreements of this kind. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has pointed out that the new agreements which will be implemented through the provisions of this legislation will be in substantially the same form as earlier agreements. This will simply mean that the agreements entered into in 1942 as a temporary expedient in time of war are to be carried forward still further into the years of peace with no assurance that the unsatisfactory relationship so clearly set forth by the Rowell-Sirois commission and by other committees which have 'examined this subject will be changed in any way. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has said that he is gratified with the measure of agreement there has been in dominion-provincial relations in the taxation fields. He has pointed out that the non-concurring provinces have shown what he described as restraint in avoiding duplication of taxation and administration. He also referred to the fact that there had been further conferences between representatives of the dominion government and the provinces with regard to this subject but that no final decisions have been reached. Those words could be used without change over and over again- "no final decisions have been reached".

speechtext:
I realize that. I repeat that those words could be used over and over again with respect to the meetings that have taken place in connection with this general subject of taxation-"no final decisions have been reached." The important decisions that need to be reached are decisions with regard to a system of taxation which will restore to the provinces that measure of independence in taxation which is an essential requirement of the effective functioning of the federal system. So far as this measure is concerned, it is the only way by which agreements can be carried forward which must be carried forward in some form by many of the provinces until some more satisfactory method of allocation of taxes is found.
When this has been pointed out on earlier occasions, an attempt has been made, without any justification in fact or from the record, to say that certain provinces have sought to retain special advantages and that it is because of the selfish attitude on the part of certain provinces that over-all arrangements have not been made. At no point in these discussions has there been a recognition on the part of the federal government that the objections that have been made, not only by the provinces which have not signed agreements but also by the provinces which have and which have indicated they had no other choice from the financial point of view, were made because there is a question of principle involved which is of very great concern not only to those interested in the provincial field of legislation and administration but also to all of us who believe in the federal system and in the continued strength of that system.
The decisions that have been sought by those provinces that have not agreed have not so much been decisions with respect to the amount of money involved as they have been decisions as to a satisfactory readjustment of taxing methods in Canada which will on the one hand avoid duplication and on the other hand give to the governments which must exercise their responsibility in the field of legislation and administration some measure of discretion with respect to taxation which will give them the real authority over the field of legislation and administration conferred upon them by the British North America Act. Those who have expressed concern with regard to the absence of any evidence of new arrangements at this time have done so with a great deal more than the amount of the payments in their minds. The simple question before us is whether the constitution is of any importance.

Is it of any importance to us that we retain the real genius of our federal system in this country? Is it of any importance that we carry forward the basic principles which were inherent in the type of federal system adopted in this country in 1867?
There are some of us who think that it is of vital and fundamental importance that the strength of the federal system be retained by a proper allocation of taxation which will go hand in hand with the other responsibilities. Those who are fearful of centralizing power in the hands of the central government remember what history teaches us where the government that taxes is not the government that spends. That can apply to a handing over of taxation rights by the central government on the one hand or by provincial or state governments on the other. Over and over again federal systems have been weakened and have collapsed where there was too great centralization of taxing power in the hands of the central government. There are also those who remember that one of the contributing factors in the weakness of the German democratic government set up after the first world war was that the central government under the Weimar constitution had become dependent upon the state governments for a substantial part of its tax resources. History teaches us the importance of imposing at the same time upon a government which spends the responsibility for being answerable for its taxation.
If the government that spends is not the government that taxes there is a loss of direct responsibility to the people both by the government which taxes for another government and also by the government that receives. The dangers of that situation may not emerge quickly. Certainly over the years that has been the situation. The measure before us simply extends an unsatisfactory situation and tends to centralize control over provincial activities in the hands of the dominion government. The best evidence of that is the fact that more and more representatives of the provincial governments and representatives of the municipalities, which are the statutory emanations of the provincial authorities, are coming here to seek special arrangements to deal with this and that problem which ordinarily could be dealt with by the provincial governments if they had that flexibility of taxing power which the full strength of the federal system demands.
One of the reasons that some concern has been expressed about the extension of grants by the dominion government in fields which are normally within provincial jurisdiction is that the experience in the past has been, where these grants are extended, that

dominion activities in these fields constantly expand until the original allocation of authority under the B.N.A. Act has been very substantially changed in actual practice.
Many people who are anxious to see education carried to the very highest possible level in every part of Canada have expressed concern about the grants for education by the dominion government, not because they are anxious to see any restraint imposed upon the ability of the local authorities to advance education in every way that is within their power, but rather because they see the possibility of a trend to place under the dominion government, no matter what political party may form that government, some measure of supervision and control which would go hand in hand with grants of that kind-such as was not contemplated by our constitution. I have supported the request for grants to our universities and I have done so because I believe that our universities perform a great national service and that in addition to the ordinary problems of education there is the necessity for an expansion of higher education, particularly in the technical fields, as part of our general plan of development and national defence. I have expressed those views on earlier occasions and shall not repeat them. Nevertheless, 1 do see dangers if this tendency should increase.
In the same way I supported the idea of a national library, although it is conceivable that there might be an argument about whether libraries are exclusively under provincial jurisdiction, ones that go beyond the extent of a parliamentary library. I do see the desirability of having a national library where the great traditions of our country may be preserved, encouraged and expanded; nevertheless I see dangers there, related to the subject now under discussion, unless we keep constantly in mind why it is important that the federal system retain that clear allocation of responsibility which preserves the vitality of a system in which unity is in itself largely the result of the extent to which diversity is maintained under that federal system, along the lines laid down in 1867.
To illustrate what I mean, I can see the danger that unless the fundamental principles inherent in our federal system are constantly recognized and preserved there might be a tendency for some to suggest the creation of a department of education under the dominion government. Perhaps it might be called a department of education and culture. When we have seen the extension of the activities of other departments which carry on activities so intensively in the provincial field, .1 think all of us should be
Tax Agreements with Provinces greatly concerned about the possibility of there being any extension of those activities in a manner that would distract attention from the fact that it was considered wise to leave under the provincial governments and provincial legislatures certain clearly defined responsibilities in certain clearly defined fields. I would hope that we would not see this tendency extended. I would hope that we would not see any suggestion to extend the central authority over education or over other matters which are now under the authority of the provincial governments, and which should remain there unless a change by agreement between the dominion and provincial governments is made in regard to any of those subjects at any time.
Changes can be made simply by invasion of a field without agreement being necessary, and that has already occurred on certain occasions. I mention this in relation to the bill now before us because I do wish to emphasize the fact that we should be expressing some concern today and some regret that we have no assurance that the conditions which have made agreements of this kind necessary for some of the provinces-and I recognize that necessity-are not going to be brought to an end, and that there will be that balanced system of taxation which will restore the full authority of the provincial governments in those fields that were intended to be fully under their direction and responsibility.
From what I have said it will be clear that I intend to support this measure because there is no alternative before us. I would point out that every province in this country has in the past indicated its willingness to enter into rental agreements of a satisfactory nature provided that there were assurance that this whole subject would be fully examined and that an effort would be made to seek a solution of the problems which have made those agreements necessary. I once again point out that these agreements were stated by this government in the first place to be temporary expedients in time of war, an attempt to meet for the time being an unsatisfactory situation emphasized by the Rowell-Sirois report; and I do hope that there may be greater success and greater determination to find a real solution to this problem.
We need to tackle the whole combined problem of taxation in Canada-dominion, provincial and municipal. The municipal problem is in many ways at the moment perhaps the most serious of all. The municipal problem is one which arises in different ways in different provinces. Each province has

Tax Agreements with Provinces its own municipal system under its own municipal laws. Each province has its own provisions for delegating the powers of taxation to the municipalities. Not one of us should overlook the extent to which there are increasing appeals by the municipalities directed to the dominion government for assistance in meeting their problem.	.
If our federal system were working as it should, there need be no appeal at any time from any municipal authority to the dominion government. Under the federal system it was intended that their relationship be a direct relationship with the provincial government. They are under the provincial government both for their legislative authority and for their administrative arrangements. That relationship should be continued. It will interfere with those relationships if they become dependent upon the dominion government for supplementary grants to assist them in meeting those obligations which are so close to the daily lives of our people.
In saying that I am remembering, and emphasizing, that it will be only through arrangements that will give to the provincial legislatures and to the provincial governments the powers they really should have that this situation can be met effectively. Our provincial governments and our municipal governments have been emphasizing the extent to which they need greater flexibility of taxation. From the domestic point of view I think there are few problems of greater importance or of greater urgency than that of taking the appropriate steps to inquire into our whole system of taxation. I think there should be conducted, under an arrangement approved by the dominion government and the provincial governments, an inquiry which will seek to advise the dominion, provincial, municipal and independent taxing authorities, with an effort made not only to simplify our taxing methods, to avoid duplication wherever possible, to reduce taxes in any way that they can be reduced at this time, but also to find a way in which the taxes will bear upon our people most lightly at a time when they are bound to bear heavy taxes in any event.
It is not only the burden of taxes that affects individuals and business in this country; it is the impact of particular forms of taxation. That matter should also be examined. I almost hesitate to make the suggestion, in view of the fact that the government have shown such an unwillingness to consider royal commissions except when it happens to be for some purpose which they themselves bring forward; nevertheless I suggest that a royal commission should hear evidence from experts in the dominion,

provincial and municipal fields, as well as independent experts from this country and from outside of Canada, in order that such a commission might make recommendations that would be helpful to both the dominion and the provincial governments.
As this measure is passed which will make it possible for the dominion government to enter into agreements which I understand have been approved by eight of the ten provincial governments, nevertheless I hope the government will recognize the need for tackling this over-all problem of taxation at the earliest possible date so that duplication may be avoided, taxes may be reduced wherever that is possible, the different levels of administration may have flexibility of taxation, and the impact of taxation itself may be in such a way that it will increase the general efficiency of production throughout Canada in every way it can. This is a time to urge that this be done, and to express once again the fact that we are called upon to pass this legislation and to see these agreements renewed for another five years without any assurance that this problem is really going to be tackled.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: COMPENSATION TO PROVINCES IN LIEU OF CERTAIN TAXES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we had before us the resolution preceding the introduction of this bill, I indicated that we would support this measure. That is our position. Despite any shortcomings there may be in the situation owing to the fact that an overall agreement has not yet been reached, we feel that this legislation certainly goes in the right direction.
It is our contention-as I pointed out on June 17, and therefore I do not need to repeat it today-that our primary concern in these matters should be not for the alleged rights of any of the governments of this country but rather for the rights of the Canadian people. We feel that any taxation arrangement akin to the set-up that we had in Canada prior to the war makes for terribly inequitable taxation. Such a system results in the situation that those who happen to be in parts of the country into which the wealth produced in other parts of the country is channelled are able to escape the taxation they should pay. After all, we are Canadians first, not citizens of particular areas in this country. It seems to me that the most important field in which we should express our Canadianism is in the economic field by an attempt to achieve as fair a distribution as we can of the wealth that is produced by the Canadian people from coast to coast.
Although we regret that an over-all agreement has not yet been reached, although we

regret that there has not yet been worked out a plan that will satisfy all of the governments concerned, and although we hope that that might yet be done, nevertheless we would not want to retreat by one iota from the position that has been attained by such agreements as have been signed between the federal government and eight of the provinces. We shall therefore support this measure.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) today once again expressed his concern for restoring to the provinces what he referred to as that independence in taxation which he regarded as an integral part of the federal system. We feel that more important than the independence of taxation which some provinces might like to have is the desirability of all of the provinces having the financial capacity to discharge their obligations to the Canadian citizens residing within their borders. A few provinces may have enjoyed that financial capacity under the kind of set-up that we had prior to the war, but certainly all provinces did not have that financial capacity. They approach enjoyment of that financial capacity under these agreements. As 1 have already said, we feel that that consideration is a much more important one than is the proposal that every province should enjoy complete independence in the field of taxation. It is our view that there are various aspects of taxation, and that there are many other aspects of public policy, by which the people in the provinces retain the control over their provincial governments. There is still plenty of room for testing the responsibility of provincial governments to the electorate in the various provinces. In fact we have had some recent examples where that responsibility has been well tested. Some were tested and found satisfactory; some were tested and found wanting. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, for these reasons and as I have already indicated, we shall support this measure.
There was one reference in the remarks of the leader of the opposition with which we agree, namely, the fact that one of the most difficult problems in the field of taxation in this country at the present time relates to municipal taxation. That is a matter beyond the control of the federal parliament; that is a matter that calls for negotiations between the various provincial governments concerned and the municipalities which are their creatures; but we feel that something is terribly needed in that field as well. Indeed, it is because of the situation in that field that there is given added impetus to
Tax Agreements with Provinces the proposal that we have made from time to time, that there should be federal aid for education.
At the present time the cost of education for the most part is levied against real estate, which we feel is unfair, for it does not accord with the principle of taxing according to ability to pay. It would be out of order for me to pursue the question of federal aid to education under this motion, but I do bring it in, in passing, to emphasize both the need for a revision of the taxation arrangements as between the provinces and the municipalities, and also as to the need for federal aid in this important field of education.
The leader of the opposition had a fair amount to say on the question of education, particularly with respect to the grants to the universities by the federal government. It is also to be noted that he has given support to the motion of my colleague, the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight), with respect to the granting of financial assistance to the various provinces for the purpose of equalizing educational opportunity across Canada. He has given that support both in speeches that he has made and by his vote, for example, on April 21 of this year, as reported at page 1463 of Hansard. In fairness to him I must admit that when he spoke on the question he expressed certain misgivings, and he tied that support to his ideas about dominion-provincial taxation arrangements; but nevertheless I think that it was an expression of his best judgment when on April 21 he voted for that motion for federal aid for education. In other words, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that we have there a recognition by the leader of the opposition of the principle which underlies these agreements, namely, that in a country like Canada, and as part of our federal system which we all support, it is essential that there be some central body with sufficient taxing authority to be able to tax the wealth of this country wherever it is made and redistribute it on a basis of fairness to the people of Canada, no matter in what part of the country they may live.
Because we believe that the rights of the people of Canada to the best that our economy can make possible are superior to the rights of individual governments, either provincial or federal, we support this measure.

subtopic: COMPENSATION TO PROVINCES IN LIEU OF CERTAIN TAXES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I remember when the first taxation agreements were negotiated between the dominion and the provincial governments we were given assurance that after the war the process of negotiating further extensions of the agreements would be terminated; that is,

Tax Agreements with Provinces that these transfer agreements would be only-temporary expedients. If I remember correctly, there were two important reasons given for the negotiations to start with. If I remember rightly the first of these was that there had to be some assurance of what the minister has called a restraint in applying taxation measure across the country so that fairness would result, particularly in wartime.
The second reason, if I remember rightly, was to put into the hands of the federal government those authorities and powers which would make it possible for us to conduct a strong and vital war effort. Well, I supported the negotiations of the first agreements because I felt that there must not be confusion in taxing matters within Canada if we were ever to put on a war effort that would be successful and that would terminate in victory for our side. I did say at the time we were negotiating the first agreements that I thought the federal government should be a little more honest in their statements. I felt that when these agreements were negotiated the federal government itself would never want to surrender whatever authorities were given over by the provincial governments. I think my fears were well founded. If I had been a betting man then I likely would have said that I bet my last shirt that those authorities and powers transferred to the federal government under the agreements would never be returned to the provinces and I believe that subsequent events have proved that my fears certainly were well founded.
At the present time we are considering an extension of the agreements for another five years. With the procedure calling the provinces together and negotiating with them in detail all parts of the agreements which had not worked out satisfactorily in the past, and revising those parts of the agreements which have become intolerable, let us say, I have no quarrel at all. I have no protest against the procedure. The provinces that did negotiate seem to be quite well satisfied with the results of their negotiations, and the details of the new agreements as outlined by the minister this morning seem to me to be perfectly acceptable, and I have heard no protest from any one of the provinces that has indicated its readiness to enter into a new agreement.
Of the provisions of the present agreements, so far as they relate to my province, I certainly have no criticism. The amount of the payments, the application of the principle of guaranteed minimum payments to the provinces, is a good provision. I think it is quite acceptable to all those provinces that have negotiated. Of course to Ontario and Quebec the principles do seem to be unacceptable.

With the provision of the adjustment payment basis I find myself in agreement. It seems to be fair. I have nothing to protest against in that regard. Perhaps I can best sum up what I feel about the bill in this way, that it is only the modification; it provides only for the extension of the present agreements on a modification basis; that is, it provides for modifications of previously negotiated agreements, but it does not in any way get down to a permanent solution of the great problem that confronts the governments of Canada, namely, a final decision on the allocation of taxation powers that could be concluded finally and for, let us say, a reasonable number of years ahead.
I think that this matter of having to come back every five years and renegotiate on the basis of agreements that were entered into temporarily to begin with is not a good thing, and I do not believe that the minister himself likes it at all. I believe in the federal type of union in this country; I think it was developed to fill a real need. In a country such as ours I doubt very much whether we could ever have satisfactory government under a unitary system. I doubt very much that we could ever have satisfactory government under a unitary system; there is too much diversity; it is too big a country. There are too many local problems to make that unitary type of government possible. And so I say I believe in the federal system as it applies to Canada. I believe in the arrangement as it was originally worked out by the fathers of confederation. I do believe that it was sound, and that the allocation of powers under the terms of the British North America Act was wise.
What I would like to see is some form of final agreement on the matter of a taxation policy as between the dominion and the provinces, settled in such fashion as to maintain the balance between the provinces on one hand and the federal or central government on the other. I would like to see that balance carefully preserved, because it was worked out by the fathers of confederation in an exceedingly wise manner, in my judgment.
Therefore we most certainly must be careful in anything we do that tends to modify the balance that was established. And in my judgment, having the federal government assume authorities that have been considered provincial for so long does interfere with that balance. It places in the hands of the central government undue authority over local governments.
I am not a centralizer; I do not believe in centralization. Obviously the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles)

has certain ideas with respect to the centralization of power in the federal government. I do not believe it is wise to take government too far from the people. The grass roots of democracy is right down in the municipality. That is where I think we should begin to decentralize, and see to it that the municipalities have sufficient authority to take care of the needs of the people right in the municipality. They are the people who know how to administer the affairs that touch their lives directly.
I am thinking now in terms of such things as health schemes and hospitalization. There is a tendency in this country to remove these things from the municipality, and to centralize their administration in the provincial governments. Now there is a move to try to centralize that sort of thing in the federal government. Well, it just will not work-that kind of centralization.
I think it has been amply demonstrated in this country as in others that there are things, things that touch the lives of the people very closely, which ought to be left exclusively to the administration of the municipalities in Canada.

I am not so sure. One thing we have to have in our mind is that no principle can be said to be absolute. I believe the hon. member for Greenwood will agree with that. What I am speaking of this morning is this:	I think that if we approach
this whole matter of dominion-provincial relationship so far as finance is concerned from the point of view of getting into the hands of the provincial governments, and through them to the municipal governments, the amount of revenue which they require to carry out their responsibilities under the constitution, we will be doing a whole lot better job than if we just think in terms of taxing powers, having to tax here or tax there.
It seems to me that the revenue which any province needs at the present time has to be assured to it and should be assured for years ahead. I do not believe it is possible for us to give them a feeling of stability by merely extending taxation agreements for five-year periods. I do not think that that is possible nor is it desirable.
I should like to see some permanent solution to this whole question. The sooner we do what the leader of the opposition, in the final minutes of his address this morning, said we should do, namely, review the taxation system and how the various taxes impinge upon the various governments, review them to see if there is not some way of coming to an agreement by which the provinces will know that certain taxation fields are exclusively theirs and certain taxation fields are exclusively the dominion's-approaching the whole matter from that point of view and reaching a final agreement and conclusion as soon as possible-the sooner we will be able to establish our provinces and our municipalities on some basis of stability and permanency.
I am concerned, as I said in the beginning, with preserving in our federal system a balance which shall not be subject to undue centralization or undue decentralization. On the other hand, we realize that there must be a strong central government as well as
Tax Agreements with Provinces strong provincial and local governments. That is desirable. It is that balance which I think we ought to try to achieve.
The leader of the opposition spoke of attempting to preserve the vitality of our federal system. I think perhaps it can best be described as vitality in a country like ours with its diversity of resources, diversity of conditions, a land that extends from the Atlantic to the Pacific. It seems to me that one of the important things we have to do is to lay down a set of policies and conditions under which we can guarantee that the vitality of our country shall never be diminished or depleted.
I think decisions have to be made soon on a more permanent basis. While we are prepared to accept the principle of Bill No. 347 which is now before us, I do not want it to be assumed that we are permanently in agreement with the idea of an extension of taxation agreements every four or five years. That is not adding to the possibility of stability in our country in any respect. We support the bill for the time being, but we do ask that the government of Canada which controls the financial policies of the whole country make every effort to come to some final allocation of powers and authorities in the financial field which will guarantee that the provinces and municipalities will have the wherewithal to take care of the responsibilities placed upon them by the British North America Act.

Mr. Speaker, I agree with those who have said we will support this measure. I just want to underline one or two things that have been said already. I think there is no doubt that we all agree with the remark that has been made that we are all federalists. We do not believe in a unitary form of government. I think it was the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe who said that the dominion after all was the child of the provinces and not vice versa. There are two things which I think are clear. First of all we are taking what was an emergency measure and perpetuating it. When I say "perpetuating it" of course I know we say that it is temporary. I think we admit it is an expedient, but after something goes on for five, ten or perhaps fifteen years it is not so very temporary and it becomes very difficult to unscramble the omelet. I think we all admit as an academic proposition that it is sound that those governments that spend money should raise the money they spend. However, we have departed a long way from that principle. Eight of the provinces have found it a comfortable and apparently a comforting thing to do.

Tax Agreements with Provinces
I have often reminded the house that we have been passing through very prosperous years when the goose has been hanging high and the provinces have received grants which I presume were very satisfactory to them. So the thing has gone along, but nevertheless I do not think anything has happened to cast doubt on that principle. If I remember right it was strongly asserted by, among others, one who was very well known in this house, the present premier of Nova Scotia.
There is one other thing I want to say. Even in spite of provincial satisfaction which seems fairly widespread, we do see one place where our present system is not really giving satisfaction, and that is in the case of the municipalities. I take it that the municipalities were not and could not be present at the discussions which took place because after all the municipalities are creatures of the provinces, and it would be almost, if not wholly, impossible to carry on discussions with them at large. Nevertheless there remains the problem that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) mentioned, and it seems to me it is a very real one. I should just like to say that in my opinion we should remind ourselves when we are doing this that, in spite of its wide acceptability, we are infringing upon a principle which I do not think has ever been satisfactorily set at nought in argument. We say we are doing it temporarily but as the years go on it is going to become harder and harder to make a change without great disturbance. There are some indications now, notably in the municipalities, that we have not solved the problem so far, and I should not wonder if, before the final solution comes, we may find, as people find so often, that we have to go back to accepted principles.
Mr. G. M. Ferrie (Mackenzie h Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words with respect to these tax agreements. I am sure that western members agree with the principle one hundred per cent. We hear a great deal about the centralizing of taxation but in a country like ours it is very hard to get away from it. The wealth produced in the western provinces is not taxable. It is the taxable dollar that you have to take into consideration, and that taxable dollar goes to eastern Canada. The taxable dollars accumulate in the place where commodities are bought. We buy goods from eastern Canada and the profits are made in eastern Canada. It is impossible for the governments of western Canada to tax those dollars. I say that all should come within the scope of the agreements in a federation of this kind. It unites the whole of Canada. We have a big industrial area in Ontario and


Quebec and then an agricultural area east and west of the two industrial provinces.
The agricultural areas must have some form of taxation that will help them and that form of taxation is controlled now by the dominion government. The provincial governments have no right to enter that field of taxation. Even if they had, the head offices of the big industries are in eastern Canada and the governments of the agricultural areas still could not tax them. The system in effect at present in some of the provinces is being condemned. That is most unfair. In the last provincial election the premier of Saskatchewan was going around the country condemning the action of the federal government so far as the moneys paid to them are concerned. I do not know what it would amount to now but before the taxation agreement was entered into all the province of Saskatchewan could collect in the form of income tax, corporation taxes and succession duties was $4,500,000. If they had the opportunity to tax today about all they could possibly collect would be double that amount. One has to take into consideration the amount of wealth produced in that province which should be taxable but cannot be because it goes out of the province. Let us say that they would have got $8 million today if they had the power to tax. The federal government is taking care of the taxing and in doing so is giving the province of Saskatchewan $26 million.
The distribution of that $26 million has prevented Saskatchewan from falling into a depression. If we in Saskatchewan as an agricultural province did not have the benefit of the grant from the federal government we could not possibly enjoy a standard of living that would compare with any part of the industrial areas of Canada. We could not tax real property in order to secure the amount of money the provincial government should have to do the job it has to do. The only way we can secure a fair distribution of the taxable dollar is under the system now being followed by the federal government. We in the west are very pleased with the way the federal government has taken hold of this matter. It is agreed that we would like to have more money but I think it is the duty of those who receive the money to give some praise to the man who has to collect it. In many parts of the country he is being condemned for high taxes. The people are paying taxes but they are having the money paid back to them and receiving services so there should be no kick coming. I wish to congratulate the

minister on the job he has done. I hope he will carry on and give us more instead of less.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened to the complaints of the west with respect to this matter. May I say that the one hope of having a geographically balanced economy for Canada is the industrialization of the west. Industrialization of the west can take place only through the development of natural resources other than farm resources. I only hope that the citizens of the three western provinces will try to forget wheat and try to remember that a great part of three western provinces is under the Pre-Cambrian shield and that a great part is now potential oil country of the greatest magnitude. Until such time as we can go farther in the west in producing natural resources other than farm produce we will not have a truly balanced economy.
There is just one other matter that I wish to bring to the attention of the minister. I have mentioned it before and I do so now very briefly because I think it is important. I refer to the matter of succession duties. Succession duties were brought in as a war measure simply and solely. They were an invasion of the provincial field but were justified as a wartime measure. To my mind collection of succession duty by the federal government is an invasion of provincial autonomy.

I have said it before but I feel that succession duties have an unfortunate result. They tend to [DOT] centralize industry in the hands of a few large corporations. When one of the owners of an individual or family corporation dies, succession duties very frequently result in the corporation being liquidated or sold to a larger corporation in the same field. That is a bad thing, Mr. Speaker, because it not only has the effect of centralizing industry in one or two larger plants but it destroys smaller industry.
I realize that small industry has been very prosperous and has been booming recently, but throughout the years if the principle persists and if succession duties are levied at extremely high levels the result will be to centralize power in the hands of a few large corporations.

I, like the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Black-more), had little intention of entering this debate. It was not, however, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) who provoked me to enter but rather the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). I see he is not in his seat at the moment; I hope he will be coming in very shortly.
As far as these tax rental agreements are concerned, I think there is very general agreement in the eight signing provinces that these agreements have been good business for the provinces concerned. It is certainly the opinion of citizens of those provinces, both in their capacity as businessmen paying corporation taxes, and as individuals paying personal income tax. I think I can go so far as to say that perhaps the businessmen in the two non-signing provinces would not be averse to paying just 5 per cent corporation tax provincially instead of the 7 per cent they pay in these provinces which have not signed these agreements. If that were all I had to say about these matters I would sit down.
However, the speech made by the leader of the opposition at the resolution stage of this debate was so extraordinary that I think some attention should be paid to it. If hon. members will look at page 3361 of Hansard, at the bottom of the right-hand column, they will find a paragraph which I will describe as the most skilful pussy-footing ever conducted in this House of Commons. So that hon. members can form their own opinion I am going to read this paragraph:
Either we believe in the federal system or we do not. * No one in the House of Commons or outside of it needs to become hysterical or to suggest that we are treading on sacred ground if anyone should assert the proposition that he believes in unitary government in this country. That argument has been made before and it will be made again. There are those who sincerely believe that Canada would be better off with a single government.
Then he goes on to imply that the federal government are those who believe that; that they believe in an all-powerful central government; that they assert that they have all the knowledge and brains in the country. For example, he says:
This government-
