I continue; page 3362:
This government may think it is in a better position to exercise judgment in regard to important matters than are some of the provincial governments. If that is their opinion, most certainly they are free to assert it; and anyone should accept that opinion as an expression of individual belief or the collective belief of this government.

Tax Agreements with Provinces
The Minister of Finance immediately interjected and made it quite clear that that was not the view of the government; that it had never been the view of the government. I began thinking to myself, why is the leader of the opposition taking such pains to state the obvious, that in this country everybody is free to say whether he believes in the federal system or in the unitary system; and who was getting hysterical about it? The hon. member for Greenwood himself in today's debate a little earlier said that we all in this country believe in the federal system of government, that it is in our constitution, and that ours is a vast country spread over 4,000 miles, over very many geographical and economic regions. Obviously, we must have a strong central government and an able, efficient local administration in these different regions. We know that every public figure in Canada with one exception has realized that. Who is the one exception? This exception was Colonel George Drew, lecturer and writer of the period from 1935 to 1941. He of course is now the leader of the opposition. He still lectures us but he is not writing.
I realize too that the hon. gentleman made another plea to this house in the budget debate, a very interesting plea. This will be found on page 1794 of Hansard when he appealed to the house somewhat along these lines: Surely all of us have said some things at some time which we would rather not have said. No person in Canada has said more things that he would rather forget than the leader of the opposition. He appealed to us at the bottom of page 1795 to forget those old speeches. All they did, he said, was to sow discord and disunity.
But not in the country. It certainly sows discord and disunity in the Tory party for Tories in some parts of this country to be reminded of what Colonel George Drew, lecturer and writer, said, and what Premier Drew of Ontario said on national issues. We all realize what a difference there is between his appeals and his performances. He asks us to forget old speeches, then issues that great little Tory pamphlet which has been circulated all over Canada, featuring the remarks made by ministers in this house, casual asides, not considered statements of government policy but truncated little asides made in the heat of debate, stripped of any context. Then he implores us to forget the public statements he has made in the past.
Well now, I am going to look back on some of the speeches he has made, not casual asides but considered speeches on his views. We all know in this house that nothing gives the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) greater pleasure than to quote his old

speeches back to us, so I am going to flatter him by also quoting him. The thing we must remember is to distinguish between George Drew the lecturer and writer in the period between 1935 and 1941, and Premier Drew of the immediately following period. In his speech on this resolution, despite his earlier plea to forget old speeches, he has referred back to a speech by Colonel Ralston in 1940 and to one by Mr. Ilsley in 1941. He also quoted from his own old speeches of that period. I therefore feel free to read from the position taken in public addresses by Colonel George Drew between 1935 and 1941; and he assured us in an early debate that these speeches are his very own; they were not speeches prepared by Rod Finlayson.
Here is an interesting paragraph from a speech in London, Ontario, as reported in the Toronto Star of February 23, 1935:
For Canada, harassed by debts, labour troubles, and conflict in company, insurance and labour laws, Col. Drew saw in one strong central government the solution, instead of an utterly mad jig-saw puzzle of ten conflicting governments. If we were starting all over again who would be crazy enough to set up ten governments in Canada?
By 1936 he had moved on in his speeches to this theme of centralization of government, as he went back and forth across the country. This is what he said before the Toronto board of trade on November 10, 1936; as reported by the Toronto Globe:
Canada must eliminate the costly inefficiency of ten governments doing, in most cases, the job of one, or else sink in the rising tide of fascism.
He was not even a good prophet. I have seen no rising tide of fascism in this country which he predicted.
Then, again in Toronto on December 10, 1938, as reported in the Montreal Gazette:
The way to get back to the ideals of confederation, to the ideal of a strong central government, is for Ontario as the largest province to sit down and say to Ottawa:
And this is Mr. Drew speaking for Ontario:
We have acquired rights it was never intended we should have. We have duplicated services. We propose to hand back to you all things of necessarily national character and retain only those things necessary for the good functioning of local government.
And again, speaking at Sudbury on January 20, 1939, as reported in the Toronto Star:
Legislation to end Ontario government services which duplicate those of other jurisdictions was promised here last night by Col. Qeorge A. Drew if he heads the provincial administration.
Declaring national unity to be the greatest single issue in Canadian public life in that it would promote development and create employment, the Ontario Conservative leader said at the present time "ten men throughout Canada are being paid to do one job." He instanced the insurance and companies departments of the federal government and the nine provinces.

Then he came down to Halifax; he was really covering the country from coast to coast, to give the Canadian people his views on the absolute necessity for powerful, central government. By 1941 he was really in his stride when, speaking before the bar association at Halifax, he said, as reported in the Halifax Herald of April 25, 1941:
"What we need greatly is to look at government from a business viewpoint," he said, "paralleling methods that a private business with a head office and nine branches would employ to promote more efficiency. Preservation of a nation's integrity must come from a strong centralization feeling," Colonel Drew continued. Canada's main problem was its decentralized government system, and the speaker declared, "solution of that problem would insure continuance of the national structure."
That is quite extraordinary in view of his recent speeches in this house. Next we have his statement before the dominion-provincial conference, the first report he made as premier of Ontario to a dominion-provincial conference, in which he said:
Decentralization of services provides the best assurance that the flexibility, vigour and efficiency of public administration will be preserved.
What a difference! What happened in this country between those statements made in 1941, when Colonel Drew was advocating a central office and branch offices; something like the Timothy Eaton form of government, with a powerful head office and branch offices all over the country just to take orders.
Why do we see this sudden change when we come to the dominion-provincial conference, this change from powerful centralization to complete decentralization. There was no change in the country in this period; it was the same Canada. There were the same provinces, with the same powers. Our national and provincial problems had not changed, and for the most part we have had the same government. The only change, of course, was that Colonel George Drew the lecturer and writer had become Colonel George Drew, premier of Ontario, in the interval.
Many people who listened to him in those days at these many public functions may have been persuaded by his eloquence and glamour to believe in centralization. When this metamorphosis from George Drew the lecturer and writer to George Drew the premier came about and he changed his views, where did that leave these people, his converts? They did not become premiers, too. What was responsible for the change? He had become a big frog in a small puddle, and was very anxious to have that puddle expanded by placing more power with the provinces. I am sure hon. members will remember the story of the frog in Aesop's fables who saw a jackass and wanted to be 55704-225i
Tax Agreements with Provinces as big as the jackass, so inflated himself up to those dimensions, finally blowing up. Premier Drew, too, wanted to inflate the importance of his position as premier of Ontario. He did not want to head one of his earlier branch offices. And that I think, is the real reason for the basic change from the great national advocate of centralization who, after a five-year speaking campaign suddenly-in one brief year-becomes the great advocate of decentralization, of giving more power to the provinces.
Now, I have said this in all kindness. In expressing these views he was very careful to preface his speech by saying "Let us not get hysterical because other people may have different views." That is quite true. If a mature mind has mature views which he expresses, and sticks to them, we must respect him. But what always puzzles us is the sudden turnabout position of Colonel George Drew, a mature man making a lot of serious speeches on a grave problem. When he made these speeches on centralization he was certainly mature physically, let me put it that way; but he has not yet told us what was responsible for his sudden about-face, from a doughty advocate of a powerful central government to being the champion of decentralization.
Let me turn now to the actual tax agreements and the points which have been raised about them. The first and the most important point is that the whole problem is based upon a formula which takes into consideration first of all the population of the country and its gross national product, what all the people in this country are producing, as Canadians.
The second important point is that these tax rental agreements are all optional. No province is obliged to sign. The provinces have gladly agreed to re-sign now that they have found this is a good way of doing business, advantageous to them and to the country. I need only remind the leader of the opposition that Mr. Anscomb, his chief lieutenant in British Columbia-he is just a lance-corporal now-was so delighted with the new agreement that he rushed back and made a public announcement before telling the cabinet. The hon. member for Peace River earlier expressed the satisfaction of the Alberta government with the way these tax rental agreements have developed. Then there is another reason, which was put forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), when he said that this is not a matter of ten warring kingdoms waging battle with some central kingdom, but that it is a Canadian problem affecting just the Canadian people who live in ten provinces.

Tax Agreements with Provinces
When you speak of a province you are not speaking of those politicians who, for the moment, form a provincial government. You are speaking of the Canadian people who live in one of our ten provinces. We have rich provinces with great natural resources and, on the other hand, we have some poor provinces who have little in the way of great natural resources. These resources do not belong to the provinces; these resources are the heritage of all the Canadian people no matter where they may live. These resources are entrusted to the provinces for management, but in the end, as I say, they are the heritage of all the Canadian people and all the people are entitled to benefit from them. These agreements make this possible.
Let me give you an example. In my province we have the greatest lead-zinc deposit in the world in the fabulous Kimberley mine. Last year the company operating that deposit paid about $40 million in corporation income tax to the federal government. That was the people's share of the profits made from mining that resource in British Columbia. As such all the people of Canada are entitled to receive some benefit from that, and when the federal government collects the tax and thus spreads it back amongst all the provinces, all the people do get benefit.
Timber is another great resource in British Columbia. The largest of our timber operations in its annual report published earlier this year reported a profit of $31 million, on which they paid $16 million taxes. That was what they paid under the corporation tax of 52 per cent. We, the people of Canada, are the major shareholders in every successful industrial operation in Canada when we take 52 per cent of their profits as taxes. Again, that resource does not belong to the people of British Columbia, it belongs to all the people of Canada; yet only the federal government can tax these profits for all the other nine provinces. There are similar resources in other provinces, although of course there are provinces which are deficient in such resources, the wealth from which can be shared by all provinces through these agreements.
The second point, which I think is a more important one, is this master of business taxation. I am going to turn to the Timothy Eaton Company, since the leader of the opposition at one time thought the best way to conduct the government of Canada was to have one strong central office with ten branch offices. Eaton's is a good example of a concern with a head office in Toronto but doing business throughout the length and breadth of Canada. We all know that indignation has been shown at various times in different municipalities by local stores which have their


own staffs and which pay local salaries and local taxes when chain or departmental stores open up a little order office, pay few local taxes or salaries but take business away from local stores. Their main profits are recorded in their head office in Toronto and are beyond the reach of either the municipality or the province, other than Ontario, to touch.
Timothy Eaton did not set up business with the idea of avoiding taxation. He set up his company in the best way he could for commercial reasons and they pay full taxes, but our tax distribution under provincial control does not put those taxes back in the areas where the profits were earned. The federal government can tax them and share the taxes back with the other nine provinces. The same thing is true of a firm like General Motors which has centralized all its operations in Oshawa. Assuming that one-tenth of their product is sold in British Columbia, it follows that one-tenth of their corporation profits should be taxable in British Columbia, that one-tenth of the income tax paid by their workmen should go to British Columbia. But because Oshawa is beyond that province, under a system of provincial taxation that is not possible. If there were ten General Motors plants across the country, one in each province, there would be no problem, but General Motors have found it profitable to have this centralization of business here in Ontario. When the provinces rent their direct tax fields to the federal government they do receive back a share of the profits earned in their province.
These tax rental agreements afford an opportunity of equalization, because the federal government does tax all industry in Canada and does spread out all those tax resources among the signing provinces and can thus give the provinces their fair share of the profits made by Canadian corporations from their operations throughout Canada and through export.
A third point which is important to us in the western provinces is that these tax rental agreements do give us some return for the benefit of the protection which the Canadian parliament has given for many years, particularly to the industries of Ontario and Quebec. I am as much a free trader as anyone, but it is quite true that in a growing country like Canada an infant industry may require a measure of protection until it can get on its feet. That protection is really at the expense of the consumer. When such an industry in Ontario and Quebec because of this protection can sell its goods in the west and make profits it is beyond the reach of those western provinces to tax those profits, but it is not beyond the reach of the federal government. In our powers of taxation in

the way of income tax, corporation tax and succession duties we do get for all Canada our fair share of those profits and by means of these tax rental agreements we spread that fair share across the country.
As the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Ferrie) pointed out, when Saskatchewan gave up the right to collect income tax, corporation tax and succession duties the best they could ever do in those fields was $4,500,000 a year. This year they are going to get $25 million from the federal government as tax rental. Even if their tax collections had doubled in the years 1939-40 down to today they are still getting far more than they could ever have hoped to collect in that province. Yet all they are getting is a fair share of the national wealth through the taxes paid by those concerns and individuals who have done well in this Canada of ours, a share based on population and national production.
We talk a lot about autonomy. The charge is made that these tax rental agreements are stripping autonomy from the provinces. I think there is a far greater freedom for the provincial government in Saskatchewan having $25 million revenue from income tax, corporation tax and succession duties to devote to provincial purposes than having $4,500,000 which was the best they could collect before this plan was inaugurated.
If there was any sign of earmarking these rental payments from the federal government to the provincial governments for specific purposes then there would be some justification for this cry. We are not stripping autonomy from the provinces when the provinces are free to use these large payments in any way they think is best fitted for their purposes within their own province. We have heard the cry that we should earmark federal funds for education, for helping the municipalities, for assistance in roadbuilding and so on, but the moment we do that we will be stripping down provincial autonomy. The best way is the way we are doing now, that is, to turn over these sums, $162 million in all this year, to the provinces for them to spend within their sphere of responsibility as they see best.
There is another important factor in the fact that the provinces are relieved from the burden of collecting these three taxes. They are also relieved from the problems that would be created by varying levels of taxation. It is one of the anomalies of our taxation system that the poorer a province is the higher they must make their taxation rates. The rich province with great industries is able to have low tax rates while the poorer province, as I say, must have higher tax
Tax Agreements with Provinces rates which in turn discourage industry from establishing in those provinces, which continues the disparity between rich and poor provinces. Through these tax agreements we have done away with eight different levels of taxation in the eight signing provinces; there is now just one federal level of taxation.
We have removed the cost of double administration, of having provincial tax offices and federal tax offices doing the same work. We are helping the taxpayer and corporations by removing the necessity for keeping two sets of books, one for the purpose of provincial taxation and the other for the purpose of federal taxation on different bases.
There is just one adverse effect which was pointed out directly by the hon. member for Mackenzie and indirectly by the other hon. members. Since the federal government is doing the major tax collection job for the eight provinces we are centralizing just one thing-centralizing all tax criticism on the head of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). The provinces are thus enabled to escape almost all criticism. A provincial leader may feel free to go around his province belabouring the federal government, especially the Department of Finance, for the heavy level of taxation, never mentioning the fact that we are collecting his province's share of the succession duties, the corporation tax and the personal income tax. However, the Minister of Finance and this government are quite willing to put up with that penalty because they know that these agreements are in the best interests of the Canadian people.
However, the payments under the tax rental agreements are only part of the benefits flowing from the tax rental plan. The only hon. member who has mentioned the other benefits promised in the green book proposals of 1945 is the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who referred to it in his excellent speech at the resolution stage. If all the provinces yielded these tax fields we promised to do more than share tax revenue with the provinces. We promised that if they would all sign we would enter the social security field by way of family allowances, old age pensions, health grants and health insurance. While all the provinces have not signed-the two major provinces with the largest tax fields have not signed- we have done a great deal toward carrying out those obligations which were mentioned when this tax rental scheme was brought up for renewal in 1945, even though these proposals were contingent on all provinces signing.
There are other large financial grants, not to the provincial governments but to the people of the provinces, through family allowances, through the new old age pension plan;

Tax Agreements with Provinces to the hospitals through hospital grants; to the provincial governments through the trans-Canada highway grants-entering fields which are really provincial fields- and through the recent grants to universities; under all of which we are sending almost $800 million over and above the tax rental payments into those provinces out of the federal treasury, again to ensure uniform appreciation by all Canadians of the wealth of this country. It is certainly a program which has met with great approval across the country. It is true we do not give all this aid to the provincial governments; family allowances and old age pensions go direct to the people. That is the point the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre made. The agreements with eight of our provinces do not mean that we are giving aid to the provincial governments but to those Canadians who live in those provinces so that they will have the same opportunity as Canadians who live in any other province.
If these things like family allowances and old age pensions were back purely in the provincial field, as the leader of the opposition would apparently like, we can well imagine the very great difference in standards between the family allowance paid in Ontario, with its concentration of industrial and commercial interests, and that which could be paid in a province like Newfoundland. Yet the old people of Ontario and Newfoundland and the young people in those provinces who receive family allowances are all Canadians entitled to the same benefits. I think that real national unity has been achieved in these eight provinces by the fact that they have signed tax rental agreements. Because of that it has been possible to go ahead with many of these programs. I see the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre bouncing up and down. It is true that it has not yet been possible to go ahead with health insurance but we have gone a long way in other respects in view of the fact that the two major provinces have remained outside the scheme.
With respect to this matter I want to refer now to another instance of opposition by the present leader of the opposition to this program of redistribution of wealth through the federal tax revenues. I am going to turn to page 1803 of Hansard for May 1. I say that most Canadians thoroughly approve of this scheme which has enabled us to have uniform distribution of national wealth to the children of Canada no matter in what province they may reside, to the old people of Canada, to the hospitals of Canada and to the universities of Canada to the amount of $800 million a year all told. Here is the real root of the opposition of the leader of the
[Mr. Sinclair.l
opposition to the tax rental scheme. I am quoting now from his famous radio broadcast of August 9, 1944, which is to be found at the page of Hansard to which I have referred. This is not a heated aside made in debate, later regretted; it is a carefully considered and prepared statement which was broadcast in the province of Ontario. It reads as follows:
This family allowance bill is an obvious bribe ... there is every reason why it should meet with approval in Quebec where there was a very important election approaching . . . Millions of dollars from the pockets of the people of Ontario will go to the province of Quebec under this measure . . . The people of Ontario will be asked to pay nearly half of the $200 million which will be needed as the initial amount to put the Family Allowances Act into effect.
Our attitude toward any measure which takes money from the pockets of the people of Ontario for the special advantage of Quebec is based upon considerations which affect that province alone. You know what those considerations are.
I have never before heard the leader of the opposition when he was so coy as in that last line. I take it the considerations are that in Quebec there are more and bigger families than in Ontario, but every one of those French-Canadian children in Quebec is just as entitled to the same national family allowance as are children in the small families of Optario or any other province. There is the heart and root of the objection of the then premier of Ontario both to the tax rental program and to family allowances; he did not want to share the wealth of Ontario with any other Canadian. I want to be fair to him so far as family allowances are concerned. Since that speech in August 1944 he has of course swung around and now lauds this Liberal government policy. He made a curious defence of that speech in the house earlier this session when he defended it by completely ignoring it and quoting from another speech he made a year later. That is a very curious defence. However, he has now completely swung around and has at last seen the virtues of this great Liberal measure because on Monday, May 19, the Canadian Press carried across the country a report of an address by the leader of the opposition in Quebec. Canadian National Railways

Reeve Jos. Rousseau, mayor of Saint Jean de Dieu, speaking on this subject, acquainted his fellow members of the county council with the encouraging remarks made in this connection by the Right Hon. (Text):
Let us have a look at the past and the future financing of the C.N.R. Bill No. 308 and this one are the Siamese twins of high finance. The former one dealt with the indebtedness of the C.N.R. to the government and the public until December 31, 1951. The latter provides for unusual ways and means to brighten the C.N.R. picture during the calendar year 1952.
In virtue of Bill No. 308, the total indebtedness of the C.N.R. to the government and the public for loans made from 1938 to 1951 was reduced by one-half. In the second place, in consideration of that so-called release, the C.N.R. transferred to the government 736,385,405 dollar shares of preferred stock of the company bearing hypothetical interest of 4 per cent. In the third place, the initial stated value of the no-par value of the capital stock was reduced to $396,518,135.06. In the fourth place, the initial value of $1,218,642,195.27 of the 5 million shares of the capital stock of the securities trust was also reduced to $378,518,135.02. To summarize that piece of legislation, the government is holding in the first place $736 million of preferred stock bearing a problematic interest of 4 per cent; and in the second place, the company has acknowledged a moral debt of $775 million in common stock.
With operating revenues of $553 million in 1950 and $624 million in 1951, it might have been expected that the management could

Canadian National Railways have made both ends meet in 1952. I cannot understand the financial policy of the Canadian National Railways. In 1937, according to the old ways of Roman law, the debts were cancelled. One-half of them were cancelled again by legislation a few days ago. Yet here we- are seeing the C.N.R. going to borrow again formidable sums of money. My fear is that they are extravagant. That is easy to see by looking at the report so extravagantly printed as compared with that modest one of the C.P.R.

The C.P.R., with
fMr. Pouliot.]
net earnings of nearly $27 million last year,
did not dare to spend so lavishly on the purchase of new equipment.

In, my view that reply, according to standing order 37, is one that is offered by a member of the opposition and not by a member on the government side. I am inclined to agree with the hon. member that the mover of a government order does not have to make a two-hour speech or a forty-minute speech in order to move the order. It is understood that when the motion is put from the chair the mover has said, "I so move". The minister may stand up and indicate to the chair by taking a bow that he does so move and one must understand that he has so moved. From that point on the Speaker puts the motion and an hon. member may stand up and offer the reply referred to in standing order 37. That is the interpretation I am, inclined at this moment to give to the standing order.
As I said, the point has not occurred before and it is difficult for me to decide. The hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) will understand that I wish to be as fair as I can

under the circumstances to him or to any other hon. member. Perhaps I could take advantage of a practice which is very well recognized in this house; that when there is a point about which the Speaker is doubtful he may ask opinions of other experienced members of the house. I would appreciate it, therefore, if at this moment other experienced members of the house would comment on the interpretation I have given, and also on the views expressed by the hon. member for Temiscouata, about the meaning of the word "reply" and who should be entitled to take advantage of standing order No. 37 in the case of a reply. As I conceive the rules in regard to debate they are related to the fact that under our system there is on one side the government and on the other side the opposition. As I understand the rules, when they use the term "reply" in response to a statement of the Prime Minister or a member of the government it is a reply by the opposite side of the house. With very warm regard for the hon. member for Temiscouata I nevertheless did not wish to have my silence taken as indicating that I was willing to accept the proposition that he is entitled to reply on behalf of the opposition. I do submit, with respect for the views of the hon. member who has sat here for so long, that the reply in this case is obviously intended to refer to a reply by some member of the opposition speaking in reply to a member of the government.

The other point I wish to draw to your attention is one that I have looked up since the matter arose. As a matter of fact I was not sure I would get it in time to be able to refer to it before you ruled; but in looking in Beauchesne's third edition, in the annotations following standing order 37, one finds in citation 219 a reference to a discussion which although not exactly the same does bear on the point now before us. It occurred in the House of Commons in 1929. I have sent to the library for the volume of Journals referred to in that citation and I have been looking through pages 394, 395 and 396 as suggested by the citation.
I find on that occasion the order before the house was a motion to go into committee

Canadian National Railways of supply. It had been moved by Mr. Robb and the first speaker was the then member for Winnipeg North Centre, my predecessor, the late Mr. Woodsworth. It appears that the Speaker on that occasion had stopped Mr. Woodsworth at the end of his forty minutes. He was asked, however, to reconsider his ruling and two days later he gave a revised ruling. The incident itself occurred on Wednesday, May 8, and the revised ruling of the Speaker of the day was given on May 10, 1929. It is a lengthy ruling which I shall not quote in full, and I want to make it perfectly clear in drawing attention to this that the situation was a little different because it was with respect to a motion to go into supply. Nevertheless in the ruling of the Speaker of that day there is this key sentence:
Therefore, Mr. Woodsworth, in order to speak longer than forty minutes, was bound to argue against Mr. Robb's motion.
There may be other rulings, but that is the only one I have been able to find and it certainly gives guidance to us today. The Speaker was attempting to interpret the meaning of the words "in reply". In fact a little earlier he said:
I have since given the most serious consideration to the interpretation of this standing order and as I said the whole question hinges on the meaning of the words "in reply" as they appear therein.
Your Honour today said the same thing. Mr. Speaker Lemieux went on to say this:
What is a reply? According to the King's English dictionary it is:-
"That which is said or written in answer to what is said or written by another; rejoinder; response."
Therefore, Mr. Woodsworth, in order to speak longer than forty minutes, was bound to argue against Mr. Robb's motion.
Then he went on to point out that since Mr. Woodsworth was opposed to the motion for Mr. Speaker to leave the chair for the house to go into committee of supply until he had had an opportunity to air the grievances which Mr. Woodsworth had in mind at that time, therefore he was opposing the motion. On that basis Mr. Speaker Lemieux reversed his decision of May 8 and decided that under those circumstances Mr. Woodsworth should have been allowed to speak longer than forty minutes.
I leave it to you, Mr. Speaker, as to whether or not the provision should be interpreted any wider than that. Mr. Speaker Lemieux did not have before him a situation such as we have today where the first member following the minister is a government supporter. He did say, however, that Mr. 

Woodsworth was speaking in opposition to Mr. Robb's motion; therefore he was speaking in reply and had the right to speak for more than forty minutes. I should like to make a brief observation in general. We do not always see that attitude reflected by ministers in the house or in committees, and when one finds that attitude displayed by a minister it is very refreshing indeed. I should like to make a comment on that fact now, Mr. Chairman, concerning the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. I do not at all mean to convey the impression that the minister accepted all the suggestions that were offered, or indeed a number of amendments that were offered to the bill. I wish to renew, on section 5, an argument I put forward in committee for some better definition of the expression found in line 29, "any crime involving moral turpitude". To most persons that expression suggests, in the first instance, offences of a type we have under the Criminal Code, and that are described particularly as crimes involving sexual offences. The minister indicated to us frankly in committee that the

expression "any crime involving moral turpitude" would mean, as to crimes committed in Canada, almost every crime if not indeed every crime under the Criminal Code.
I offer now an example-and it may be a rather extreme example-by way of illustration of what this may mean. Bear in mind, if you will, that when this expression is applied to a person in Canada, as the minister has indicated, it would be treated as the equivalent of practically any offence, whether an ordinary offence or an indictable offence under the Criminal Code. As applied to an act of some person outside of Canada, as the minister indicated, the department will interpret it to mean any offence that would be regarded as an offence against the criminal law, according to Canadian standards of criminal law.
I put this extreme case as indicating the need, both in this and in one or two other sections we will come to, for a much closer definition of what is meant. I take the case -because it is fairly obvious-of a person who comes to Canada from Ireland. It is discovered after he has been here one day short of the necessary five years required to acquire domicile that prior to his departure from Ireland he got into an argument with his neighbour over the fence, and poked the neighbour in the nose. That would be a case of common assault, assuming that there was no aggravation in the offence. The magistrate before whom the unhappy man was haled might take a light view of the offence, and, while it would be within his power to register a conviction, he might impose nothing more than a nominal fine or, indeed, he might direct a remand for sentence, or might suspend sentence.
After the individual in question has been in Canada four years, eleven months and twenty-nine days it comes to the attention of the immigration branch that this person was convicted of the crime of common assault before his entry into Canada. This immediately makes him subject to deportation. That is the law as created by the bill before us.
If the expression "any crime involving moral turpitude" is to be considered in the way the minister has indicated-and that is the way the department will construe the expression in the present act, because it is not a new expression-then this individual has rendered himself liable to deportation. I do not suggest the present minister is going to do anything so arbitrary or, indeed, so foolish as to direct the deportation of a man under those circumstances. But the fact of the matter is that under this bill he could. That individual is liable to deportation.
Immigration Act
I think when we are legislating we do not want to legislate in such a way as to make it possible to have a result as absurd as that.
I had proposed in committee that we should seek some better expression, some clearer definition of the sort of thing we have in mind, than this broad term "any crime involving moral turpitude".
In the light of the position taken by the minister in committee, and the decision of the committee, the bill comes back to us with this expression remaining in it. I want to record my view that this is a defect in the bill and that something much more definite in the way of a definition is required.

I should like to make an observation on subsection 3, clause (c) which permits the special inquiry officers to issue commissions or requests to take evidence in Canada. The committee has added the words "in Canada" and to that extent has narrowed the scope of the section in the original bill. But I wish to express the view that I sought to put forward in the committee about the care with which a power like this should be exercised.
There is no power in the present Immigration Act to permit any officer of the department to issue a commission to take evidence. As you well know, in legal proceedings in all the provinces the issue of a commission to take evidence is not something that is obtained as a right; it is something which the courts permit only where a sufficient case has been made out to justify it. For the first time this bill proposes to confer upon every special inquiry officer under this act the power to issue a commission to take evidence anywhere in Canada.
Something might be said for taking evidence in other parts of Canada for use in connection with deportation proceedings that are pending against an individual, but having regard to the position in which many of these persons will find themselves I think this is a power which should be exercised only in clear cases. Think of the position of an individual awaiting deportation. In the first instance, he may be suffering from the disability of language; he may understand neither English nor French. In the second place, he may be suffering from a state of confusion in which many immigrants find themselves when arriving in Canada. It seems to me that where evidence is being used against him which may result in his being deported the least he is entitled to is the right to have the witness cross-examined, to confront the witness face

Immigration Act
to face. That right should be most carefully preserved. The great difficulty about taking evidence on commission is that it may be taken far away from the place where the individual may be held while the deportation proceedings are continuing. He may be timid, he may be confused, and he may be unaware of his rights.
In such cases I think injustice could be done to the unhappy individual if any arbitrary use is made of the power to take evidence on commission. As I have indicated, the committee has circumscribed this power to the taking of evidence on commission within Canada only. But even with that limitation in many circumstances the power could be used to the detriment of the individual facing deportation proceedings. I urge upon the minister a very sparing use of such power.

We see in subsection 3 of section 28 that deportation may be ordered by a special inquiry officer of a person who falls within the various clauses of section 19 to which I made reference. The minister has indicated in the comment he has just made that provision exists in the present act that makes the individual in the extreme case to which I have referred liable to deportation. He has said that discretion is created by the new bill in favour of the minister to exercise clemency-and I think most of us would say common sense-in a situation of that kind and permit the individual to escape deportation. However, I think we ought to go further than that. The fact of the matter is that if this legislation passes in the present form we are legislating to this effect, that the individual who on the eve of completing five years' residence in Canada after lawful admission commits the offence of common assault makes himself liable to deportation, and only exercise of a discretion by the minister permits that individual to escape deportation.
In my submission the grounds upon which the individual renders himself liable to deportation are much too extensive. They are much too broad. We should raise the floor in a case of this kind. I am quite in accord with the idea that the minister should have discretion in proper cases because there is going to be need of discretion being exercised in many cases if the law is to be written in terms as rigorous as some of those we have before us. The fact of the matter is that in my submission no individual who has given a good account of himself in Canada for the period I suggested, four years, eleven months and twenty-nine days, after being lawfully admitted, should be rendered subject to deportation simply because he commits what is nothing more than a very simple offence. It is not an indictable offence, and in the case I mentioned it might be under circumstances as to which the magistrate,

while feeling he might be obliged to enter a conviction, would take anything but a serious view of what had happened. I cannot think that parliament, in proceeding seriously about its task of legislating with respect to this very important subject of immigration, wants to place anybody in a position like that, where he is dependent upon favourable exercise by the minister of his discretion under the act to escape deportation.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, while this bill was before the special committee on veterans affairs, as you have pointed out, and was reported without amendment, I might say that it was carried on division in that committee. This is an extremely important bill to a most deserving class of our war pensioners, namely the amputation cases. The reason it was carried on division was that many of the members of the veterans affairs committee felt that the increase provided by this bill with regard to clothing allowance was not enough.
I might point out, Mr. Chairman, that there has been no change in the allowances made to amputees for clothing since 1925. In that year, for any amputation of the leg above a Symes' amputation, so-called, the allowance for wear and tear on clothing was $54. Since 1925 twenty-seven years have elapsed. We all know of the great increase in the cost of clothing during that time. As a matter of fact, it was
Pension Act
pointed out to the committee that since 1925 the cost of clothing has increased by about 100 per cent or more. Many members of the committee felt that the allowance provided in this bill, namely a 33J per cent increase, was not sufficient and was not fair to these amputees.
In 1925 the allowance made to amputees other than those with Symes' amputations was $22; and with the increase of 334 per cent as provided in the bill this amount will be increased to $30. There were three classes dealt with. First there were those with other than Symes' amputations. The second class were those with amputations at or above the wrist; and the third class were those who had to use other appliances. It was pointed out that the wear and tear on the clothing of these classes was very great. There is extreme wear and tear on the clothing of amputees and those who have to wear these other appliances.
The $54 provided in 1925 was equivalent to providing an extra suit of clothes for these men. To provide an extra suit of clothes for those same veterans in 1952 costs in the neighbourhood of $80 to $100. Many of us felt that a larger amount should be allowed than that provided in the bill.
I should like to point out that of these leg amputations above the so-called Symes' amputation, there are 3,070. This was brought out in the evidence before the committee. The annual liability to the country before the proposed increase was $165,780. The increase as proposed in the bill will mean $55,260. As to those with arm amputations, we were advised in the committee by the witnesses from the department that there were 1,294. The present cost is $28,468, and the proposed increase would mean $10,352. As to those with other appliances, there were 2,452. The present cost is $115,244. The bill means an increase of $61,300. The total increase under this bill will be $126,912. I might say that the total cost at the present time for these classes of amputees and those who wear appliances is $309,492. If this amount were even doubled it would mean a cost of only $618,984 or not quite two-thirds of a million dollars.
I point this out to show that, with regard to this class of veterans and with regard to this particular allowance, the cost is extremely small. I felt, as did other members of the committee, that we could very well have doubled the amount of $309,492 and not made the cost very great as far as the country was concerned. It is hardly necessary for me to say that this is a most deserving class of veterans. They are the most helpless class of veterans that we have. As we

Veterans Legislation
know, their clothing is subject to tremendous wear and tear during the year. I simply call this matter to the attention of this committee because, as I say, when the bill was carried in the veterans affairs committee, it was carried on division, and those were the particular reasons upon which we divided in that committee.

Section agreed to.
Sections 2 to 4 inclusive agreed to.
