On section 1-Short title.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCES FOR WAR VETERANS AND THEIR DEPENDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this bill was before the committee for some days. While there was very little controversy in respect of the other bills passed by the committee, there was considerable debate and considerable controversy so far as this particular bill was concerned.
The committee will recall that when the resolution was before the house many weaknesses were pointed out, and they were again emphasized in committee. Unfortunately the amendments were not made along the lines we had hoped, and the weaknesses in the act when it went to committee are still there. This, I may say, is a matter of great disappointment to many members of the committee, as well as to veterans organizations Who presented the case to the committee on behalf of recipients of war veterans allowances. It is also a disappointment to all veterans across this country.
This is a most important bill. We had expected that the legislation before us in the special committee would have been before a committee on veterans affairs over a year ago. As a matter of fact we felt that when the Pension Act was being considered and amended, the War Veterans Allowance Act should have been amended as well. We were pleased, however, when at the last session

of parliament we were told there would be a war veterans committee at this session.
We had every reason to believe that this most important legislation would have been corrected this session. However, the bill as presented to the committee made very few changes in the act. One of the benefits of having the bill before us was that it was a consolidation, a feature which met with the general approval of all members on the committee.
There is one section in the bill which has given general satisfaction, and that is the provision allowing veterans to receive allowances during certain months of the year and to work in other months. It was felt, however, that the encouragement given to some other veterans was not sufficient.
We were very pleased to learn that veterans employed in different types of work are giving satisfaction. In that connection I should like to read from the report of the work of the Department of Veterans Affairs. At page 18 I find set out a summary of welfare services, where there is reference to the employment of veterans and to the satisfaction they are giving their employers. At page 18 I find this:
A review of the progress made during the year shows that the work of casualty rehabilitation and welfare has been efficiently carried out with many cases being closed as successfully re-established in civil life, and with fewer disabled veterans unemployed than ever before.
It has also been ascertained that the incidence of dismissal of disabled veterans from work on the grounds of inefficiency is negligible, thereby proving that placements have been soundly made in jobs where, notwithstanding the disability of the veteran, his courage and determination has enabled him to turn out volume and quality equal to those who are not disabled.
That is a statement which I know will give great satisfaction not only to members of the House of Commons but to all veterans across Canada. On the same page, the welfare services branch reports on the older veterans as follows:
The principal need of the older veteran in reasonably good health is steady, gainful employment and, when to obtain and retain such work becomes a problem, the branch is prepared to take an interest. In various ways the branch has stimulated the interest of employers and community groups in the value of the older veteran properly placed in employment and, in co-operation with national employment service, believes that substantial results have been achieved. During the year, national employment service recorded employment registrations by 45,756 older veterans and at March 31 the number unplaced was 9,519 as compared with 12,284 at the end of the previous year.
That indicates clearly to me, as I am sure it must to all hon. members, that not only is the older veteran capable of working in many instances, but also he is most anxious to get employment whenever it is possible. I

was interested in a report made by Mr. Ryder of the research department in which he pointed out that from a research made it was found that the health, of the older veteran was much better than had been expected. I do not know what the object of the research was, but he pointed out to our committee that men of the age of 55 years who were receiving war veterans allowance on account of some disability or on account of poor health had a greater death rate than civilians in the same age group. He pointed out also that the death rate of recipients of war veterans allowance 60 years and over was lower than that of the corresponding civilian age group. I think the inference which possibly was meant to be drawn was that the war veteran had not aged as much as had been expected due to his war service.
I think it should be brought out at this time that no such inference should be drawn. In the first place, as was pointed out in the committee, those men who are 60 years of age and over and who served in the first war were the best of the young men in the country at that time. They were more physically fit than any others; they were the cream of the crop, as it were. They were hardier than many of the men who were unable to pass the physical examination for overseas service and who on that account stayed home during the first war.
There is another argument that could be used for granting war veterans allowance. When these men came back from the first war they were not in the same position economically as were those who had stayed at home. As a matter of fact I believe the war veterans allowance was granted on that point as well. These men came back and found that there was not the employment for them they had expected. They found that those who had stayed home were well established and that it was more difficult for them to become rehabilitated. There is a great difference between the men who served in the first world war and those who served in the second.
Then again, no action had been made after the first world war to provide educational facilities as was done after the second war. Many of the men who came back took land under the soldier settlement board, and we know they had a very hard time. They went through two depressions and also the second world war, and it was more difficult for them to become established than it was for those who had stayed home.
This brings me to my criticism of the present act. We criticized the present act chiefly because it did not increase the ceilings to the 55704-227J
War Veterans Allowance Act extent we thought they should have been increased. Under the old ceiling a single man was permitted to earn $125 over and above his war veterans allowance while a married man could earn $250. Under the new ceiling, both single and married men are entitled to earn only $120 over and above their allowances. Instead of increasing the ceilings there has been a decrease in the cases of both the single and married man. We felt that there should have been an increase in both instances.
A number of cases were presented by the Legion where particular individuals would suffer. One case was that of the older veteran who possibly with the help of his wife or someone else was able to hold a position as janitor or do some job of that nature. The low ceiling would allow him to earn only an extra $120 a year; therefore it would be impossible for him to take a job of that kind. Then there was the case of the older veteran and his wife who might have a room to rent for perhaps $4 or $5 per week. Again he would be prohibited from doing this because of the low ceiling. There was also the case of the man who had been able to earn a retirement pension of from $20 to $50 a month. He would not be eligible because of the low ceiling. The worst case of all was the man with a disability pension, say 50 per cent. If this man was married and totally unemployable he would get very little assistance under the War Veterans Allowance Act; if he was single he would receive none at all.
It was felt that these few cases illustrated clearly the unfairness of leaving the ceiling or the permissible amount which the veteran was allowed to earn at only $120 per year. The matter was thoroughly discussed in the committee, and it is not necessary for me to dwell further on that point.
The second matter to which we objected strongly was the amount of the allowance, namely $50 for a single veteran and $90 for a married veteran. It was pointed out to us, as we have pointed out in the house on numerous occasions, that the increase should have been based on the cost of living. Since 1939 the cost of living has increased by something like 82 per cent, whereas the increase in the war veterans allowance is only 33J per cent.
Those are the two main objections we have to the bill. We think veterans are not being treated fairly or justly in this respect, and we feel the attention of the committee should be called to these matters. I know there are other members who are going to speak on the bill along the same lines, and it is not my intention to take any more time.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCES FOR WAR VETERANS AND THEIR DEPENDENTS
speechtext:
I too was a member of the special committee, and most of the things

War Veterans Allowance Act that we would ordinarily say we said there. However, there are a few matters to which I should like to refer. The minister has already indicated that several amendments are being made to the bill. In my opinion a lot of discussion will have to take place on the bill as we discuss it clause by clause. At this time the things about which I am concerned are the amendments that were not introduced and that we will not have an opportunity to discuss as we consider the bill.
The first amendment that I thought should have been made and which was not made is an amendment of the act to include the widows of imperial veterans whose husbands passed away before they were able to comply with the twenty-year residence qualification.
I had figures indicating that the problem was not very big and there would not have been much money involved. After the many times this matter has been discussed in the house I am disappointed that the act was not amended at this session to include the widows of imperial veterans who did not meet the residence clause. We object strenuously to what is not done for those who are already getting something; but the position such a widow finds herself in is very difficult because she receives nothing. The fact that she lost her husband before he had resided in Canada for twenty years does not improve her position very much, because the widow has been here the necessary time. She still has to eat and provide a home for herself in Canada and, as somebody remarked in the committee, the body of her husband is still in Canada. As far as he is concerned his bones are interred here and will remain here. Rather than a strict legal application of the act humanitarian consideration should be given to the widow who gets nothing at the present time. As I said before the cost would not be so great, because the figures presented to the committee indicated that not many cases are involved.
My second disappointment with respect to the amendments that were brought forward arose because of the fact that no amendment was introduced to include veterans of world war I who saw service in England. There are a considerable number of them, and in my opinion when the government amended the War Veterans Allowance Act to include veterans of world war II who saw service in England they immediately created discrimination. That discrimination should have been removed. We argued the matter in the committee but the government appeared to be adamant at this time that that recommendation was not going to be followed. I was very sorry to see these two matters not dealt with in the amendments the minister is presenting at this session. In my opinion the

act has been improved. The computing of the war veterans allowance on a monthly basis, without any reference to the income that may be earned by a veteran able to take seasonal employment for four, five or six months of a year, is a move in the right direction. There are many older soldiers who cannot take steady employment in heavy industry but who can do light work of a seasonal nature particularly in the summer months when the weather is good. Thus they are able to earn something, and then they can go back on the war veterans allowance when that type of employment is no longer available without the income they have earned being held against them on an annual basis.
I think that is a big improvement in the act and gives considerable latitude to the exservice man who finds himself in the position of not being able to work all the time.
There was a lot of discussion and several motions in the committee with respect to the schedule. Many of us thought the rates in the schedule were too low. They certainly did not meet the request of the Legion in their presentation to the committee, but again the government appeared to be adamant in the stand that this was as far as they were going at the present time.
We can have a lot of discussion on the clauses of the bill, but I want to say one thing now. There was a proposition made before the veterans affairs committee by a doctor from Vancouver. I spoke about the matter in the committee and I mentioned it in the house on second reading of the bill. I refer to the proposal that appears to have emanated from Vancouver where they have set up a geriatrics division in one of their institutions. The idea is that older veterans who are inmates of the institutions across Canada are going to be taken under the wing of this new organization and are going to be given some training. In the case of Vancouver the officials who are giving the training are working on a voluntary basis with the co-operation, as this gentleman told us, of the community chest people in that city.
I cannot agree with his presentation of the matter. We have to ask ourselves this question. To begin with why are these older veterans inmates of these institutions? Why was it necessary for any veteran to make application to the veterans affairs department asking that the department admit him to an institution and look after him so far as his meals, room and general maintenance are concerned? Why did he do that in the first place? He did it because he was no longer employable. He was certified as being unemployable by a medical authority or he was

over 60 years of age. Otherwise he would not have been receiving the war veterans allowance.
Having the war veterans allowance, why did he seek to become an inmate of an institution? He requested to be allowed to enter the institution because he was not getting enough on which to live on the outside. That is the answer. Some of them have been veterans care cases off and on over the years throughout the country, but apparently this medical doctor has devised a scheme of instituting a geriatrics division. Older veterans will go into these institutions, and they have to be psychoanalysed. They range in age from over 60 to about 70 and they are broken down. They are not employable. They are in these institutions because they cannot live on the outside. In Vancouver under the program sponsored by the community chest organization- they are very benevolent people-a geriatrics division has been set up, and apparently with the general sanction of the veterans affairs department these older veterans are going to be psychoanalysed to determine what their aptitudes may be for employment. They are going to find employment for them.
The doctor told us that there was one old gentleman in the institution whom they rehabilitated. He could do a little typing, so they made his fingers nimble again and sent him to a bush camp to type for the office manager. That was one case, but to my mind the whole idea is ridiculous and as far as I am concerned I am opposed to it. In the first place the veteran who is in that condition, the older veteran who goes into an institution, has reached the end of the trail. There is nothing outside for him. If he received enough by way of war veterans allowance to pay for a room and a bite to eat he would not have to become an inmate of that institution. He is a definite charge on the Canadian people and a responsibility of the Canadian government.
I object to any system whereby it is proposed to take men in this age group and ascertain whether they should go back to work somewhere just to get them out of the institutions. I want the members of the veterans affairs committee to think about the matter. I definitely object to them becoming in any sense of the term linked up with the charitable organizations of this country. It certainly is not the prerogative of any charitable institution in this country to become involved in veterans affairs. For that purpose there is a special ministry of government. There is a large department of veterans affairs and it extends clear across the country. There are investigators, there are hospitals and there are staffs across the country which
War Veterans Allowance Act are adequate to care for the needs of veterans in any category. I object to any attempt to turn the institutions established for veterans of this country in the direction of working through some other scheme that involves charitable organizations across the country.
If you want to do something for the older veteran who has been necessarily institutionalized because he cannot find employment and live on the outside, the thing to do is increase the rate of war veterans allowance so that the men can pay for room and board outside, and you will not have any of them in institutions.
On that particular angle I speak to you, Mr. Chairman, and through you to the minister, because I can very easily see what is going to happen. If you have a hundred or two of the older veterans institutionalized in Vancouver, Halifax, London or Toronto, or any of our large centres, and you start on this system of geriatrics what you are going to see happen is just this. They will be picked as orderlies in the hospital-no pay, of course-and they will be required to sweep floors, polish wards, make beds and do the work of a general orderly. Somebody determines whether they are fit for that type of work and they will say: If you do not do that type of work, out you go. We were going to rehabilitate you by giving you a job mopping floors, but you would not do that.
Before we get into that kind of organization I strongly urge the Minister of Veterans Affairs to take a square look at the problem and determine whether he has sufficient staff to look after the needs of veterans. If he has not, then he should increase the staff rather than seek the co-operation of charitable organizations across this country and let them get into veterans affairs in any way, shape or form. Let the minister build the department up if he has not sufficient staff to find jobs for these older fellows.
With conditions as they are and with the average condition of these old soldiers who have had to become institutionalized, the idea here is far-fetched and ridiculous, in my opinion. If there is anything these men can do, if they have any aptitude and there is employment they will find it. I think they are in a better position to determine what their capabilities are than the average welfare officer whose intentions may be good but whose ideas in my opinion are pretty far-fetched.
I just wanted to make this statement because I notice that very few people have been saying anything about this angle. I got the impression that some of the members of the committee at least were impressed and thought this was a good idea. To my mind it is not a good idea, and before we conclude

War Veterans Allowance Act this discussion I want the minister to tell the house exactly what the department has in mind and to what extent they are considering the organization of this geriatrics proposition across the country.
There are a few other matters in the bill on which I wish to speak, but I will reserve my remarks for the clauses of the bill.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCES FOR WAR VETERANS AND THEIR DEPENDENTS
speechtext:
I think I pretty well indicated my feelings on this bill when I spoke in the debate on the resolution. I agree that it is a great improvement over the act as it was before but, as I stated at that time, I do not think it goes quite far enough. I also stated that I believed any increases in war veterans allowance should be based on the cost of living index. The relationship of the present rates with those of 1939 is not in proportion at all when compared with the cost of living index today.
X also agree that section 4 is certainly an improvement. It does give the veteran who is able an opportunity to take seasonal or part-time employment. It encourages him to take employment when he can get it and contribute that much toward the welfare of the country. However, I do think they should get some sort of increase in allowance so they can have at least a reasonable standard of living. I think the maximum income allowed is too low. They can earn very little outside the actual allowance, and in my opinion that is an error. They should be encouraged to take what employment they can get because there are jobs open which do not pay enough to warrant a person working at them full time, and these men can handle those jobs quite nicely.
As previous speakers have indicated, we would like to see included wives of imperial veterans whose husbands died prior to having twenty years' residence. It does seem a shame that a woman should be penalized simply because her husband died beiore residing here for the required time.
As I said earlier when speaking on this bill, the property allowance could be increased to some extent without causing any hardship on the government. Although the present allowance is sufficient to cover a modest home, it should be increased, I think to such an extent that these people can at least live in a comfortable dwelling for the time they are receiving an allowance.
As I said before, this is an improvement and apparently the government are learning to crawl toward the ultimate goal. We just hope they will keep on improving this act as they go along, possibly speeding up the improvements at the next session.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCES FOR WAR VETERANS AND THEIR DEPENDENTS
speechtext:
This bill is of great importance to the war veterans of Canada because it is a complete revision of the War Veterans Allowance Act. There has been no such revision for many years and the veterans of the country have been looking forward to a measure of this kind for a long, long time. It is important, therefore, that the measure as passed by the house now should be in the best possible form. One other reason that is the case is that it is very unlikely that there will be any changes of much consequence in the years that lie immediately ahead.
The bill as it comes back from the special committee on veterans affairs has been improved in several different ways, and I am extremely glad to be able to say that such is the case. There are, however, still two serious defects in the bill, and I come to them at once. The first is that the amount of the war veterans allowance has not been increased to the extent that it should have been increased. The second is that the permissive income or, in other words, the amount of income that a veteran may have or earn over and above the allowance, has not been made sufficiently high. I propose to deal briefly with those two defects.
First, as to the amount of the allowance, may I say this. At the present time the single veteran who qualifies for a full war veterans allowance can get $40.41 per month. Under the changes made in this bill he will be able to get $50 per month, an increase of $9.59. The married veteran drawing a full war veterans allowance will be able to get $90 per month whereas he now can get only $70.83. That is a difference of $19.17.
In addition to the war veterans allowance itself there is a special fund known as the war veterans allowance assistance fund from which a single veteran may draw an additional $10 per month and a married veteran may draw up to a maximum of $15 per month. Payments in many cases are not made in cash but by way of purchasing clothing, furniture or something that may be urgently required.
This assistance fund is based entirely on need. I have here the notice which was sent out by the department when the assistance fund was first set up two or three years ago. It stresses the fact that this fund can be drawn upon only in cases of need. This means, of course, that a veteran must first establish his qualification for the allowance itself which involves a means test, and it will continue to be a means test under this new bill. Then to get help from the fund he must pass a second means test.
The proposal made by both of the great veterans organizations of Canada-and I

refer to the Canadian Legion and the National Council of Veterans Associations in Canada-was that there should be established in this new bill a war veterans allowance of $60 a month for the single man and $120 per month for the married veteran. I have here the brief filed with the special committee by the National Council of Veterans Associations. In dealing with this question they have this to say:
Supplementation of war veterans allowance rates through the assistance fund for those who are unemployable and unable to supplement through casual earnings was at the outset regarded as practical and justifiable. However, in practice, it would appear that the supplementation in addition to the original means test attached to the war veterans allowance assistance fund has carried a secondary means test which serves to confuse and discourage worthy applicants.
Then they go on to recommend that the assistance fund payment be absorbed into the war veterans allowance itself and that there be payable a total of $60 for the single veteran and $120 for the married one. The Legion have made exactly the same submission. It so happens that their great national convention took place while the sittings of this special committee were being held. At that convention the Legion officials received a unanimous endorsation of the brief which had been submitted to our committee. There is therefore no question whatever as to where these great veterans organizations of Canada stand on this question. They believe the figures should be $60 and $120.
Then to come to the second main defect which is the amount of permissive income; at the present time, under the law as it now stands, that amount is $125 for the single veteran and $250 for the married one. In other words he can earn or get by way of interest or in any other way up to $125 or $250 over and above his maximum allowance. For some strange reason this new bill we are considering tonight cuts that figure to $120 for both the single man and the married one. In their brief the Legion dealt with that change in the following way:
. . . the Canadian Legion feels that a retrograde step has been taken in proposing the reduction in permissible income from other sources to $120 a year for both single and married veterans instead of the previous $125 and $250. An increase, not a reduction, seems indicated.
The National Council of Veterans Associations also dealt with the matter. They said:
It is quite obvious that the extremely limited ceiling applicable at present and contemplated in Bill No. 181 now before the house and affecting war veterans allowance, has not been sufficiently realistic in facing the problems of living costs under present-day conditions. In fact, the extremely low ceiling is reminiscent of the traditional poor-law philosophy-that the unfortunate should be grateful for a pittance.
War Veterans Allowance Act
This question of the amount of permissive income is of great importance. The Legion pointed that fact out by giving examples. I am going to read these examples to the committee because they clearly show how important it is to allow a higher permissive income. Here is the first case they mention:
First, there is the individual not physically able to do a full day's work. He may be competent, or with his wife be competent, to handle a part-time job such as janitor of a school or church, watchman, or some other work which provides regular employment but the labour is light and the pay is small.
He cannot qualify as a casual labourer for his earnings are regular, his income from this work may be smaller than war veterans allowance alone would give him, and neither earnings nor war veterans allowance taken separately is sufficient to support him.
Then they go on to quote from a letter written by the wife of a veteran in Alberta, as follows:
Whilst my husband was in hospital our minister offered us a three-room house with light and water and $50 a month. I told him we could not accept the salary, but would oe glad to accept the house and light free in exchange for caretaking of church property, but that we had better consult the W.V.A. board first. We have just received the letter tonight, and believe it or not, if we take this house and light and donate our work to the church the W.V.A. will deduct the rent value from his allowance.
Then the president of the Legion went on to read from the Legion brief:
I am quite sure the members of this committee will sympathize with the lady when she exclaims: "In the name of God what kind of system is this?"
Then the brief deals with another type of case, as follows:
In addition to recipients who can do work such as this, there are families who, finding it impossible to live on W.V.A. and the husband unfit for work, the women have to go out to work, and this at an age when that certainly should not be required of them, to earn enough to keep the home going. Meagre as their earnings seem to be they are more than W.V.A. would bring, but not a great deal more. Here the husband has a heavy psychic burden as well as his physical disability to bear.
Then they say:
Then there are individuals, thrifty and provident, who over the years have earned for themselves a small retirement pension of $25 or $50 per month. Not enough to live on, but enough to be a very great help if W.V.A. were permitted to bring their income up to a subsistence level.
In other words, if the ceiling on permissive income were raised, then these veterans and their wives would be able to get a decent income on which to live.
Then the Legion dealt with the case of pensioners in these words:
Finally, there is the disability pensioner, who is entitled to W.V.A.
Because, of course, his pension is so small. I continue:
The last pension increase he received did him no good, for he suffered a corresponding decrease in W.V.A.

War Veterans Allowance Act
That is what happened last year with these particular veterans, as we pointed out during the debates.
Many of these men find their war wounds an increasingly grave handicap, and these, coupled with their physical disabilities, may make them completely unemployable. Under the proposed legislation-
They are referring to this Bill No. 181.
-a 50 per cent disability veteran, if married and totally unemployable, can get but little assistance under the W.V.A.; the single man none at all.
I repeat, it is of the greatest importance that there be an increase in the permissive income allowed to these veterans.
All we need to do is compare the permissive income allowed under old age assistance. I hold in my hand the Old Age Assistance Act which was passed last year. It applies of course to people between the ages of 65 and 70. Both single persons and married persons are allowed a permissive income of $240 a year over and above the amount they get by way of assistance. There can be no justification for treating the veteran more harshly than the treatment given the recipients of old age assistance.
You may wonder, Mr. Chairman, why we did not have these changes made when the bill was before the committee, and of course that is a very proper question. Well, the answer is that we did our best to have the bill perfected in committee, but we were unable to make any progress. We ran into a government stone wall. I have here the proceedings of the committee for May 23. On that date we commenced to consider this bill by sections and my colleague, the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough, moved this amendment:
That the committee recommend that the government give consideration to introducing legislation during the present session of parliament which will give effect to the representations submitted to the committee by the Legion and national council of veterans that the rates of allowance and the maximum total incomes set out in the schedules to Bill 181 should be increased.
There was an amendment to that motion moved by one of the government members on that committee. It was finally ruled out of order by the chairman, and a different amendment was substituted for it by another government member, which is to be found in the proceedings of June 5.

the hon. member is a stickler for the book. maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCES FOR WAR VETERANS AND THEIR DEPENDENTS
speechtext:
My point is, whether it was ruled out of order or withdrawn, a new amendment was substituted by another government member, and it read as follows:
That all the words after the word "that" to the end of the question.-
He was here referring to the motion moved by the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough.
-be struck out and the following words be substituted therefor: the committee recommends to the government continued and sympathetic study of the needs and requirements of recipients of war veterans allowance keeping in mind the recommendations of the veterans organizations in that respect and particularly with regard to permissive income.
To that amendment the hon. member for Royal moved a subamendment as follows: ... by adding thereto the following words: and give consideration to introducing legislation accordingly at the present session.
That subamendment was ruled out of order by the chairman who is the parliamentary assistant, who just interrupted me. We appealed his ruling. It was supported by a straight vote of government members, with all the opposition members of all parties voting against the ruling and the hon. member for Fraser Valley abstaining.
When we got down to the sections of the bill an amendment was again moved by my colleague, the hon. member for Royal, recommending that the government give consideration to increasing the amounts in the schedules to this bill, which contain the figures both of allowances and of permissive incomes. That too was ruled out of order by the chairman of the committee. We again appealed his ruling. Again every Liberal member voted in support of the ruling with the exception of the hon. member for Fraser Valley, who voted with the members of the three opposition parties. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, we did our best to see that these changes were made at the present session

because time is of great importance to these veterans. These are front-line Canadian veterans having to exist on a subsistence level, and time means a great deal to them. They may die by next year if they cannot get a proper allowance.
Certainly they should not have to wait a year to have the ceiling raised. The amendment moved by government members in the committee would indicate that there is some possibility of the government making that change. Well, it will be a great tragedy if the change does not come before another year. We had that experience last year with pensions, the refusal of the government to make a proper increase in the pension rate. There was delay. Then last fall, finally, an increase was put through. It may be that we will have to go through the same procedure with regard to war veterans allowances.
I cannot urge upon the government and my fellow members too strongly that these changes should be made now, before this session closes. The rates should be increased to $60 and $120, and the amount of permissive income should be increased as well.
It seems to me that, for the first time, this war veterans legislation is now being influenced by social assistance legislation. Attempts are being made to place the veteran on the basis of the civilian social legislation. The Legion pointed that out in their brief when they said:
It appears from the legislation before you that the government, in suggesting rates and allowances, has been influenced to some extent by legislation in the field of social assistance. However we would strongly suggest that this proposed legislation affects men and women who have served this country honourably and well in time of war.
Those words sum up the situation very clearly. If this legislation is not put into proper shape before the close of this session, the government may well find itself faced with a request to abolish the means test in connection with the war veterans allowance. After all, the means test was abolished for civilians at 70 years of age, and the war veterans allowance was made payable at 60 on the basis that the veteran who had frontline service was pre-aged to the extent of ten years. It will not be easy for the minister to justify a refusal to abolish the means test in the case of veterans on war veterans allowance and to allow the veteran at 60 to have whatever amount of income he can earn.
There is nothing more one can say. The case is there for a proper increase, and for a proper amount of permissive income. All we can do is leave the problem on the doorstep of the minister and the government. If they wish to be fair with these old comrades of ours, who in the first great war helped
War Veterans Allowance Act save this nation, and fair to the younger men who did it again just a few years ago, then there will be no hesitation in bringing the allowance up to the right amount at the present session, as well as bringing up the amount of permissive income.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCES FOR WAR VETERANS AND THEIR DEPENDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as a member this session of the committee on veterans affairs, let me say I agree in principle with everything said this evening by the hon. member for Royal, the hon. member for Cape Breton South and the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra.
I fully realize that Bill No. 181, respecting allowances for war veterans and their dependents, has been considered by the government, and sets out what the government proposes to do in respect of war veterans allowances at this session. That is clearly indicated. I hope, however, that the shortcomings of the measure pointed out in the briefs of the various veterans organizations, and by members on the veterans affairs committee, will be considered by the Minister of Veterans Affairs, by his department and the government, and that those shortcomings will be remedied.
I would hope that we would have another committee on veterans affairs at the next session of parliament, that these shortcomings would be rectified, and that the government would bring in a new act to include all the legitimate requests made by the various organizations interested in the matter. It has been pointed out tonight that the war veterans are receiving something far short of what they should get.
I would hope in particular that the widows of imperial veterans, who in many cases resided here almost the required 20 years, might receive proper consideration. We know of cases where husbands have died just before completing 20 years of residence. I think of one case in particular where there had been residence for 19 and a half years, just a few months short of 20 years. Yet widows in that position are denied any assistance. Surely that is something that should be rectified; indeed, it should have been done at this session.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCES FOR WAR VETERANS AND THEIR DEPENDENTS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, as a member of the veterans affairs committee may I support what has been said by the hon. members for Vancouver-Quadra and Royal, who have said many things I would have liked to say. I heartily support the proposals they have made, and trust the minister was listening carefully so they may bear fruit.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCES FOR WAR VETERANS AND THEIR DEPENDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was not a
member of the special committee on veterans affairs at this session. Perhaps therefore I

War Veterans Allowance Act may be permitted to voice my disappointment at the results the committee was able to achieve.
The advantages and disadvantages of the bill have been explained. One is pleased to see that this seasonal allowance is being introduced. But I do venture to say that while a number of veterans who are recipients of war veterans allowances will be able to get some form of seasonal work during the summer months, far more recipients of war veterans allowances will not be able to get those jobs because, even in the summer months, jobs for elderly men are limited.
I regret to see that the increase in the allowance is not greater. The total income now permitted for a single man, as I understand, is $720 a year, and for a married man $1,200. Those amounts seem pitifully small. When one thinks of other pension schemes in existence and being considered at the present time, he cannot help feeling that the committee lost all sense of proportion. If the house approves of this meagre increase, and the meagre amount of permissive earnings, then I feel it, too, will have lost all sense of proportion.
The claim may be made that these veterans did not make any contribution to their allowances, pensions or insurance schemes, whatever they may be called. I say these men made their contributions by service. They have not been in a position to make large contributions to any generous pension scheme. I hope before this session closes the members of the House of Commons will bear in mind the amount that they are now "generously" allotting to these old soldiers.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCES FOR WAR VETERANS AND THEIR DEPENDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not feel I would be doing my duty if I did not get up and say a few words on this bill because in the last few years I have had considerable to do with veterans affairs. I want to thank the government for going as far as they have gone with this legislation, but in my opinion the bill still lacks some sections which should have been included. One of the sections which I think should have been included is one dealing with veterans who served in England during the first great war. Today many of those veterans who do not happen to be pensioners are unable to obtain this allowance because England was not considered to be a theatre of war.
Those men may have been kept in England through no fault of their own. I know from experience-this is a matter which we may have to face in future years-that many soldiers were kept in Canada during the second world war through no fault of their own. They were good, reliable soldiers but their commanding officers would not permit IMr. Pearkes.]

them to go over because they required good men here. Many veterans of the first world war may have been kept in England because of their ability to fill certain positions, because of their ability to carry on their jobs. I feel that they should be given some consideration in the legislation now before this committee.
Another point I should like to take up is that which has been dealt with by previous speakers. I contend that the ceiling, if you wish to call it that, is not high enough. In fact I submit there should not be any ceiling at all. We should permit these veterans to earn whatever money they are able to earn at whatever work they can get. They would then feel that they are contributing something toward their own support, that they are part of our economic life, that they are not just cast off and depending entirely on charity. That is the way you make them feel when you tell them that they can earn only so much.
If a married veteran has a family-I happen to know a few who have-$1,200 is not enough to permit them to more than barely exist. I do not know what the process is, but I would hope that this legislation could be reconsidered and amended, at this session if possible, so consideration could be given to veterans who served in England during the first war and to also raise the amount of permissible income a veteran may earn, either married or single.
There are many veterans who would like to do some work. They would like to think that they were at least helping to earn their own living. Under this legislation, if they are going to receive a war veterans allowance, they hardly dare go out and earn anything. It is like the story of the old woman related by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. Some of these men just cannot understand this legislation. They cannot understand why they are not permitted to work and have the allowance when they are willing to work.

I think the minister should clarify the purposes of this section which deals with exempt income. Clause (f) reads:
(f) receipt of money or assistance from any province or municipality by way of mothers' allowance or by way of relief to dependent children.
War Veterans Allowance Act
Any outsider reading that clause will automatically assume that a widow in receipt of veterans allowance may also receive a mothers' allowance from the province. The minister will remember that I asked in committee whether this section dealing with exempt income was discussed with the provinces and if the provinces indicated they were willing to pay a widow a mothers' allowance if she was in receipt of a war veterans allowance. The answer I got, partially in the committee and partially off the record, was to the effect that there was consultation with the provinces and that in British Columbia and the western provinces generally there was some understanding. The understanding is to the effect that the total amount of the war veterans allowance as laid down by the War Veterans Allowance Act and the total amount of the mothers' allowance paid by the province will not both be paid. The war veterans allowance can supplement the mothers' allowance or vice versa. However, I understand that in the provinces from Quebec east no understanding was arrived at. I assume that a widow who may be on mothers' allowance in such a province and who can qualify for war veterans allowance will automatically cease to draw mothers' allowance when she applies for war veterans allowance.
Of course she is better off financially under the War Veterans Allowance Act. However, in the interest of saving members and departmental officials a lot of correspondence on this matter I should like the minister to make a brief statement explaining paragraph (f) of subsection 1 of section 6 so far as exempt income is concerned, because as it reads now the assumption is that one can draw both.

There are some provinces where mothers

War Veterans Allowance Act can receive both the war veterans allowance and the payment under provincial legislation. Others have not seen fit to do that, and we can do no more than pray that some day they will permit payment as is done elsewhere.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCES FOR WAR VETERANS AND THEIR DEPENDENTS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Cape Breton South raised the question of the widow of an imperial veteran who cannot qualify for war veterans allowance because her husband died before he had been here for twenty years. I suggest to the minister that he give consideration to having section 30, subsection 4 (b), which defines the residence qualification, changed to make it a domicile qualification. If it were worded to the general effect that the imperial veteran was domiciled in Canada before the 1st January, 1931, that would meet these cases and I think would be more in line with the actual wishes of previous veterans affairs committees. If the minister will recall, the group of imperial veterans who were


intended to be covered were the group who came here in the twenties. They had all come here by the end of 1930. I think there were practically none who came here after that time. There may be some coming now. but there were practically none between 1930 and the end of the second world war.
What we really were trying to do was cover the group who came here in the twenties; but instead of wording the definition to provide for those who were domiciled here by the end of the year 1930 we put it the other way around because the provision was only made in 1950, and we said it would apply to those who had resided in Canada for a total period of at least twenty years. There is no similar definition in the War Veterans Allowance Act. In other cases the test of domicile is used. For example, the minister will find that expression used in line 4 on page 12 of the bill. It refers to the imperial who was domiciled in Canada before the first war and then went overseas and served in the imperial forces. He has had eligibility throughout, the test being that he was domiciled in Canada before he went overseas in the first world war. I believe the test for this other group of imperials who came here after the first world war should be based on whether or not they were domiciled here before the end of 1930. If that were done the widows would all be covered and no widow would be ruled out provided her husband was actually domiciled in Canada before the end of 1930. I would ask the minister for his comments on that suggestion.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCES FOR WAR VETERANS AND THEIR DEPENDENTS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, following the remarks of my hon. friend, I will be very glad to consider the suggestions he has made. I am not aware of the full implications of such a change, but to my mind it would involve a change in principle. I would not like to commit myself at the present time but I will certainly consider his remarks.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCES FOR WAR VETERANS AND THEIR DEPENDENTS
speechtext: The suggestion is that you strike out the words "has resided in Canada for a total period of at least twenty years" and substitute "was domiciled in Canada prior to January 1, 1931."

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCES FOR WAR VETERANS AND THEIR DEPENDENTS
speechtext:
This is an ingenious device conceived for the express purpose of breaking the ceiling'which was put on the legislation when the imperial veterans were brought under the War Veterans Allowance Act. It is improper to suggest that was defined by the committee which wrote that legislation or the house which adopted it. The twenty-year clause was designed, perfected and brought forward by those people who sought

that benefit. As my hon. friend knows, because he was on the committee, those people came forward and said that was their final proposition. There had to be some definition under which they could qualify for benefit.
As my hon. friend knows, and as all the members of the committee know, benefits of this legislation flow from the veteran himself. Consequently if he is not qualified his dependents do not qualify.
I do not want to elaborate at the moment, but it is not correct to say that a change in the qualifying period would not be a change in principle. It definitely would be a change in principle. I am not arguing whether it should or should not be done at the present time, but I am saying for the benefit of the house that it does involve a change in principle, an abandonment of the principle upon which provision was made for wives of imperial veterans.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCES FOR WAR VETERANS AND THEIR DEPENDENTS
speechtext:
I do not suppose the imperial veterans association gave any thought whatever to the widows. The matter probably did not cross their minds. The twenty-year clause is primarily related to the year 1930. That is why twenty years was put in, because they were going back to the year 1930. The legislation was passed in 1950 and the twenty-year residence qualifications was made then.
I am not trying to bring in any ingenious methods to break any ceilings or do anything of that kind. I simply suggest the test should be on domicile here before the end of 1930.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCES FOR WAR VETERANS AND THEIR DEPENDENTS
speechtext: I do not dispute that, but my point is that we should not argue or pretend that it does not mean an abandonment of the original principle behind the legislation. It does.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCES FOR WAR VETERANS AND THEIR DEPENDENTS

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCES FOR WAR VETERANS AND THEIR DEPENDENTS
speechtext: I did not say that.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCES FOR WAR VETERANS AND THEIR DEPENDENTS
speechtext: The parliamentary assistant stated a few moments ago that all the benefits of the act flow from the veteran himself.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCES FOR WAR VETERANS AND THEIR DEPENDENTS

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCES FOR WAR VETERANS AND THEIR DEPENDENTS
speechtext: Yes. If the act were amended to make the suggestion of the member for Vancouver-Quadra operative that would in no way change the principle. What we are arguing about now is the widows' position. If the veteran had lived in Canada for twenty years he would have been eligible for war veterans allowance.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCES FOR WAR VETERANS AND THEIR DEPENDENTS
speechtext:
That is not in dispute.
War Veterans Allowance Act

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCES FOR WAR VETERANS AND THEIR DEPENDENTS
speechtext:
By an act of God he did not live in Canada for the full twenty years. He was short a few months and passed on. That does not in any way change the benefits that flow from him.
We have already amended the act to make it applicable to the Canadian soldier who passes away in Canada. The benefit of the act is transferred to the widow. The need of the imperial veteran's widow is exactly the same as the Canadian veteran's widow. The benefit is a right that flows from the soldier to the widow because she is in need at this time. We are setting up a discrimination as between the need of the ex-imperial widow in Canada and the Canadian widow; and the pension should go to her because of need as it goes to the Canadian veteran's widow.
If the minister took the proposal under consideration and it were enacted we would remove an injustice and a discrimination. I do not think the amount involved is sufficient to have us quibbling year after year about this. This did not start yesterday in the veterans affairs committee; it started a good many years ago. We have included here what amounts to a discrimination and an injustice, and changing it would not affect the principle as I see it. I cannot help but feel that the application of this suggestion would save a lot of time in the future. I know the member for Vancouver-Quadra is going to continue to talk about this, and I am going to help him. The committee even passed it up in their recommendations to the house. The committee did not recommend anything on it.
Can the minister say that his department will take this under consideration, and may we hope that at the next session we will be able to avoid this discrimination and injustice?
